articles.title_orig: US tries to restrict Chinese offshore computing capacity
articles.title_zh: US tries to restrict Chinese offshore computing capacity
articles.content_orig:
Some €510 billion ($559 billion) have been invested into AI infrastructure across Malaysia since February 2025. The consulting group Fitch Solutions has opened 125 data centers in Malaysia to serve the global digital economy. The sector is booming in the western Malaysian state of Johor where, according to Malaysia's Digital Ministry, 16 of 27 new data centers are located.
The government in Kuala Lumpur hopes the investment will create numerous new jobs, up to 90% of which are expected to be filled by locals. The advantages of the data center sites include low electricity prices for energy-intensive computing and good links to international submarine cables.
Major US technology companies have also set up along the Strait of Malacca. Amazon and Oracle have each invested $6 billion, while Microsoft and Google have invested $2 billion apiece. In early November, Google's parent company, Alphabet, announced additional investments of $15 billion.
"Malaysia's vision is not only to build an economy that uses artificial intelligence , but also one that uses AI creatively,” explained Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo in a statement that was tellingly published in Chinese, which is not an official language of Malaysia.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Data center growth in Southeast Asia is part of the race for technological supremacy in artificial intelligence. The US has restricted the export of high-performance chips , such as those produced by US tech giant Nvidia , to China. It has also tried to block the sale of the advanced lithography machines used to manufacture microchips that are made by Dutch manufacturer ASML.
Since Chinese chips have yet to reach the same technological standards as others, some Chinese companies are testing an alternative model in that they legally purchase or lease capacity in other countries. They can thus rent access to US chips that have been installed in systems in Malaysia, for example, and develop their AI models from abroad.
In October, the Institute for Progress (IFP), an independent think tank in Washington, warned that Southeast Asia was becoming an offshore hub for Chinese AI enclaves. It estimated that by the end of the year about 24% of China's total computing power came from remote access to overseas data centers, three-quarters of which were in Southeast Asia. This was predicted to rise to 31% by the end of 2027.
The IFP said that though "US AI chips hosted in overseas data centers are a significant source of compute for China," they were "difficult to size."
It explained that "Chinese entities can rent GPUs [graphics processing units] as a service from cloud providers or lease data center capacity overseas, directly from developers or through intermediaries. Cloud providers and data center developers rarely name their customers or disclose how much capacity each uses, and Chinese companies disclose little themselves."
The Chinese giant Alibaba Cloud currently operates six data centers in Malaysia — three in Johor and three in the greater Kuala Lumpur region, with the most recent one opening on November 19.
The company has invested $53 billion in data centers in total, including in South Korea , Thailand , the Philippines and Mexico, as well as Malaysia. TikTok's parent company also operates data center capacity in Johor.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In early October, Tencent, another multinational technology conglomerate, which is based in Shenzhen, signed a five-year $7 billion contract with Oracle, allowing it to use computing capacity equivalent to 100,000 modern AI chips for training artificial intelligence. The company was supposed to pay 30% upfront.
The deal fell through a few weeks later, however, and both companies have remained silent about the reasons. According to media reports, there was pressure from the governments in both Beijing and Washington. China wants to develop its own chip industry, whereas high-ranking US officials reportedly raised security concerns with Oracle.
In mid-2025, the US threatened to impose an additional 25% tariff on Malaysia imports "to prevent circumvention of export controls on chips," according to the Chinese consulting firm Equal Ocean. "The Malaysian government quickly responded by opposing illegal resale practices and introducing licensing requirements for the transshipment of certain high-end chips."
Washington is now stepping up its efforts. On the same day that US President Donald Trump met with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping at the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, China last week, the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency of the US Department of Commerce, issued new rules with regard to remote access to advanced AI chips and servers.
It said that the goal was "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests." The restrictions pertain to data centers that provide significant computing capacity to companies with ties to countries in "Country Group D:5 or Macau."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
According to US export regulations, the D:5 group includes China, Russia, Iran and North Korea and others. In future, companies will have to conduct more thorough checks to identify the ownership and control structures behind their clients.
Washington has also introduced new licensing requirements for advanced semiconductors destined for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil . Subsidiaries of US companies are exempt.
"The US is not only reviewing which countries will receive AI chips in future but also wants to have a say in where the chips are used, who operates them and which customers they serve," explained Chinese industry expert Xu Sanlang. "This means that data centers, which have been providing remote computing capacity to Chinese clients will have to comply with these restrictions in future."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.content_orig:

Chinese consumer rights advocate Wang Hai has spent three decades exposing counterfeit goods and seeking compensation for buyers. In recent months, he left China fearing he was a target of the authorities, but now he is stranded in South Korea with his family, facing possible deportation home.
Wang, a well-known campaigner against counterfeit goods, said China invalidated his passport and South Korean authorities rejected his asylum. The United States also revoked his tourist visa, narrowing his options for leaving South Korea and deepening his fears of being sent back to China.
Chinese authorities launched a campaign against organized crime in July, saying they would target “malicious compensation claims.” Since then, authorities have arrested at least 100 people for allegedly extorting businesses through anti-counterfeiting work or consumer compensation claims, according to official statements reviewed by The Associated Press.
Wang said the arrests made him fear he could be next, prompting him to leave a country where official Chinese media had once praised him for his role as anti-counterfeiting activist.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs told The Associated Press it was not aware of Wang’s case. The Ministry of Public Security did not respond to a request for comment.
The quagmire in which Wang, 53, and his family have found themselves has drawn concerns from rights advocates over China’s efforts to target critics abroad and the narrowing options for people seeking refuge in the U.S.
“The Chinese government’s practice of transnational repression is well documented, including in South Korea,” said Yaqiu Wang, senior China researcher at Human Rights Watch, based in Washington , and “there is no doubt that the Trump administration has created a far more hostile environment for immigrants, and even visitors.”
Wang spoke to the AP from South Korea about his situation and has appealed the rejection of his asylum application in that country.
The activist fears he will end up in jail if deported to China
The activist said that he arrived in South Korea in late September with his wife, 8-year-old daughter and infant son.
Wang said he believed Chinese authorities were targeting him and that dozens of his staff members were arrested and questioned. Some remain in detention, he said. One staffer had his passport revoked while traveling from Thailand to Singapore last month, according to him.
“The very same job has suddenly morphed from being praised into something associated with organized crime — it’s absolutely surreal," said Wang.
Asked what he is afraid of if he is sent to China, Wang didn’t hesitate: “I would definitely spend the rest of my life behind bars.”
A notice reviewed by AP showed South Korean immigration authorities rejected Wang's and his family's applications for refugee status. AP also reviewed the U.S. Embassy email that revoked his visa, in which U.S. authorities told Wang that new information made him inadmissible to the U.S. or ineligible for a U.S. visa but did not provide specific details.
The U.S. State Department didn't immediately respond to the request for comment.
He was once praised as a ‘woodpecker’ rooting out fraud
Wang became a household name in China in the 1990s for exposing counterfeit goods, an increasingly widespread problem as the country’s market economy expanded rapidly and consumer protection oversight lagged.
In 1998, Wang joined a roundtable discussion with then-U.S. President Bill Clinton during his visit to Shanghai. Wang told Clinton he had been viewed as “immoral” at home, according to a White House transcript.
Chinese state media, however, largely portrayed him favorably, calling him “China’s No. 1 anti-counterfeiting activist.” Professional consumer advocates were compared to “woodpeckers,” rooting out problems in the marketplace.
Wang ran a rights-protection company in Beijing for about 30 years and a testing laboratory supporting anti-counterfeiting work for five years. He said both were forced to close after many of his staff, including three lawyers, were arrested in September.
The closure of his offices came after China launched its campaign against organized crime. Authorities said some people were using consumer complaints, lawsuits or threats of exposure to extort money from businesses through what officials called “malicious compensation claims.”
Some lawyers say consumer rights advocates play a positive role by exposing illegal practices, pressing businesses to address problems and helping authorities enforce regulations.
“The fact that some individuals engage in these activities as a profession or as a source of income does not invalidate the legitimacy of such social oversight itself,” said Zhang Yansheng, a Beijing-based lawyer.
After fleeing China, Wang seeks a new home with freedom
Wang’s consumer advocacy began more than three decades ago, when he suspected two pairs of Sony headphones he bought at a Beijing department store were counterfeit. He bought the remaining 10 pairs and secured compensation of twice the purchase price. It was widely celebrated on Chinese state media as a pioneering case of consumer activism.
He went on to run his own company and testing lab, helping consumers seek compensation and pushing for stronger consumer protections.
Wang and other advocates also pushed for a minimum compensation payment of 500 yuan ($75) for consumers, a proposal later incorporated into a revised consumer protection law in 2013.
His most recent case involved helping cherry farmers in the northeastern city of Dalian get compensation after they bought fake pesticide. He said Dalian police later arrested and detained around four dozens of people including the cherry farmers, two lawyers who represented the farmers, and Wang's staff.
Wang said he has since focused on researching asylum options and hopes to settle in the U.S., Canada, Britain, Australia or New Zealand, seeking what he called “real law enforcement and freedom” to “get away from China's transnational repression.”
After his U.S. visa was revoked, Wang is seeking resettlement in Canada with the help of a human rights organization.
Fearing arrest by Chinese authorities even outside China, he said he and his family mostly stay indoors in South Korea. He said his bank accounts in China have been frozen, leaving the family in financial difficulty, and his 8-year-old daughter is struggling with her mental health because she cannot attend school.

articles.title_orig: FedEx cargo plane runs off Miami International Airport runway, causing ground stop during Thanksgiving travel
articles.title_zh: FedEx cargo plane runs off Miami International Airport runway, causing ground stop during Thanksgiving travel
articles.content_orig:
A FedEx cargo plane ran off a runway at Miami International Airport amid wind and rain Wednesday night, prompting a temporary ground stop during one of the busiest travel days of the year.
According to an FAA advisory, departures bound for Miami were grounded until at least 9:45 p.m. Preliminary reports indicate a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 cargo plane went off the runway, prompting the halt in incoming air traffic.
The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said it responded to the runway at MIA at approximately 8:40 p.m. and found the cargo plane.
Neither of the two people on board was injured, and responding emergency crews from both  MDSO and Miami-Dade Fire Rescue reported no signs of fire or smoke.
MIA posted on X, confirming the incident and saying it happened at Runway 26R, and that all runways are closed except for Runway 9R.
A FedEx aircraft overran Runway 26R at Miami International Airport at approximately 8:40 p.m. All runways are closed except for runway 9R. @MiamiDadeFire units have responded, and there are no reported injuries. Passengers scheduled to travel tonight are encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport. We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations.
Minutes before flights were set to resume and the ground stop is expected to be lifted, the FAA also posted on X about the incident, confirming that the FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 departed from Frederick W. Smith International Airport in Memphis.
At the time of the incident, rainy conditions had reduced visibility to 7 miles, with a 13 mph tailwind reported at the airfield.
An airport employee who witnessed the aftermath and asked not to be named said the crew appeared to struggle to slow the aircraft on the wet pavement before it veered onto the grass.
"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," the employee said.
The worker noted that the overrun occurred on the airport's shortest runway, raising renewed concerns following a September Amazon cargo plane crash that killed five people.
The disabled aircraft prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a brief ground stop at Miami International Airport, leaving some Thanksgiving travelers waiting on the ground for hours before flight operations resumed.
"I'm kind of shocked," traveler Dennis Pastorizo said. "I didn't think that a delivery plane would cause a two-hour delay for a flight to the other side of the country, especially on one of the busiest [travel days] of the year."
FedEx issued a statement to CBS News Miami about the incident that says:
"FedEx Flight 910 from Memphis to Miami experienced an issue upon landing Wednesday evening at Miami International Airport. We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."
The FAA announced Wednesday night that it is investigating the incident.

articles.title_orig: Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every American child
articles.title_zh: Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every American child
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX said Wednesday it will donate one share of the company's class A stock to every active Trump Account , and CEO Elon Musk would personally match the gift.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
The White House announced in October that nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created, including more than 60 million through auto-enrollment. It's unclear how many are considered active.
Eligible children must have their account claimed to enable contributions from family members, friends and employers, and to receive the government's one-time $1,000 seed contribution. Auto-enrolled children can receive philanthropic contributions without a parent or guardian claiming an account, according to TrumpAccounts.gov.
Representatives for SpaceX and the U.S. Department of the Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for further details about the planned gift.
SpaceX Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell had previously agreed to make a personal gift of over 2 million SpaceX shares to Trump Accounts, with eligible account holders expected to receive them in December .
In October, Elon Musk posted on X that he would give a share of SpaceX to every kid in America next year.
Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.
Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027.
Since the July 4 launch, families and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts . Total deposits now sit at more than $9 billion, CNBC first reported.
Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria.
The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations , a move officials have said is meant to encourage more philanthropic gifts.
Contributing stock can benefit donors, who are able to avoid capital gains taxes triggered by selling appreciated stock. But families can face restrictions related to selling that donated stock. The policy also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies.
Under U.S. Department of the Treasury guidelines, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17.
SpaceX shares have been under some pricing pressure as the company negotiates a possible merger with Elon Musk's automaker Tesla . The companies have established two special committees to handle merger negotiations, and hired advisers for a potential mega-deal.
CNBC's Kevin Breuninger, Kate Dore and Jess Dickler contributed to this story

articles.title_orig: "No One Gets Left Behind" - CDPR On The Witcher 4 Releasing On All Platforms At The Same Time
articles.title_zh: "No One Gets Left Behind" - CDPR On The Witcher 4 Releasing On All Platforms At The Same Time
articles.content_orig:
This week, CD Projekt Red and Sony announced an exclusive marketing deal for Ciri's upcoming title, The Witcher 4 . It's raised some concerns online about the fourth outing potentially being a "timed-exclusive" for the PS5, but thankfully, this won't be the case.
CD Projekt Red's co-CEO Michal Nowakowski confirmed this to a fan via social media , but his response about how "no one gets left behind" (in reference to previously announced versions of the game) appears to have upset some Nintendo fans, as there's currently no confirmation of a Switch 2 version.
"All the platforms release at the same time - PS5, XB, and PC. No one gets left behind."
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
The Witcher 4 was unveiled for PS5, Xbox and PC in 2024 , and there's been no mention of a Nintendo release since then. While this doesn't completely rule out a Switch 2 port in the future, Nintendo fans have noted how the "Switch 2 is clearly getting left behind" in this case.
Of course, we'll remain hopeful given CDPR's strong support of Nintendo's platforms in the past and more recently during the Switch 2's launch window. The fourth game, powered by Unreal Engine 5, also isn't expected until 2028 , so anything could happen between now and then.
The Polish studio previously worked its magic (with the help of Saber Interactive) during the Switch generation, with an "impossible" port of Witcher 3 . Most recently, Switch 2 players got Witcher 3 Remastered , and this is set to be followed by the new expansion ' Songs of the Past ' in 2027 . CDPR also did a "preem" job on the Switch 2 version of Cyberpunk 2077 .

After eight years of Socialist-led government under Pedro SÃ¡nchez, Spain is at a crossroads.
Snap elections are taking place on Sunday 29 November, and voters face a choice of continued left-wing rule or a conservative-led government, with the likely support of far-right Vox.
Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o's conservative People's Party is narrowly ahead of the Socialist PSOE in most polls.
He has spoken of Spain being probably at "the most significant moment in our country for the past 50 years", and he aims to "repair the state, regenerate democracy, reunited the nation and recover Spain's ambition and self-esteem". But it is unlikely he could do anything without the backing of Vox, who are third in the opinion polls.
For more on FeijÃ³o and who else to watch in this election - read here .
Spain has a population of almost 50 million, and almost 39 million people have the right to vote for the Congress and the upper house, the Senate. The polls open at 09:00 (08:00 GMT) on Sunday and close at 20:00 (19:00 GMT), when the first exit polls come out.
SÃ¡nchez called this vote eight months early after MPs rejected planned changes to Spain's housing laws.
He was responding to nationwide protests after an 87-year-old woman called Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her rented flat in Madrid and later died.
But his government lost the support of a centre-right party called Junts from the north-eastern region of Catalonia which sought to protect the rights of property owners.
Housing remains one of the hot-button issues for voters, but they are also focused on the high cost of living, corruption and immigration.
Spain saw its first general strike for 14 years this month over a shortage of housing and high rental costs
Spain's property prices and rents have soared by more than 80% from 2015 to 2025, and wages have not kept pace.
Spain has a combination of high demand and scarce supply: the Bank of Spain estimates 700,000 homes are needed to ease the pressure.
The result is that millions of Spaniards have little chance to buy a house, while they live in fear of eviction if their rent is increased. On 11 November, four million Spaniards were galvanised into joining the first general strike since 2012, according to the unions.
Pedro SÃ¡nchez has embraced housing reform as a big campaign issue and left-wing parties have promised rent controls and protection against eviction, while the right is focusing on building more homes, tax breaks for homebuyers and planning deregulation.
SÃ¡nchez's wife BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez has played an important role in the election campaign
Support for the Socialists is down from 2023, but even then he came second in the race and relied on the backing of other parties, mainly on the left, to stay in power. This time those other left-wing parties, in particular the Broad Front (Frente Amplio) have fallen back and the big questions now are more about FeijÃ³o's conservatives.
"It is a demobilisation of the left. Sanchez's party is not doing well," says Jacobo Ramos Folch, Policy Analyst and visiting professor at the University of Navarra.
"That lack of majority is really a reality â and the rise of Vox. What is changing that shift of majorities is the rise of Vox."
Vox have been around since 2013 but polls suggest this time they could almost double their 33 seats in Spain's lower house, the Congress.
Their big themes are "national priority" â putting Spanish citizens first for subsidies and welfare, along with repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain.
Pedro SÃ¡nchez (left), Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o (centre) and Santiago Abascal (right)
Migration has become a key challenge for Spain, and Alberto NuÃ±ez Feijoo has accused his rival of being a "problem for Europe when it comes to immigration" after the influx of tens of thousands of migrants into the exclave of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco in July.
This month too, the Canary Island of El Hierro has seen record arrivals, with 2,000 people landing there on 24 November. Abascal has spoken of "another invasion".
And yet a recent CIS survey put it far behind housing, cost of living, healthcare and working conditions.
The PP and Vox have bitterly criticised the Socialist-led government for a drive to legalise unauthorised migrants this year that attracted 1.2 million applications.
FeijÃ³o's party wants to see more controlled immigration. Vox has called for mass deportations.
Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
FeijÃ³o has accused the Socialists of being "the most corrupt party" that Spain had ever seen, and a number of cases have involved SÃ¡nchez's inner circle and family.
People should distinguish between real and "fictitious" corruption allegations, says el momento mÃ¡s trascendental.
His former transport minister JosÃ© Luis Ãbalos has been given 24 years in prison over multiple corruption offences.
Leading party figure Santos CerdÃ¡n awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.
SÃ¡nchez's wife BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez faces trial for alleged misuse of public funds and using her marriage to further her academic career. She denies wrongdoing. And his brother David SÃ¡nchez has been banned from public office for nine years for administrative misconduct.
FeijÃ³o has made clear his objective is to form a majority and make "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox. As far as a coalition is concerned, he says he will respect the will of Spanish voters, but maintains Abascal has never talked to him about running any ministries.
The PP leader is clear that Vox's national priority policy would run counter to Spain's constitution and European Union treaties: "No-one can sign illegal agreements."
Even if they were to go into coalition, Camino Mortera-Martinez of the Centre for European Reform, and a former European affairs adviser to the Spanish prime minister is not convinced Vox would wield much influence.
"They're not going to get any of the core ministries. They're not going to get defence or home affairs or foreign policy or economy," she told the BBC. Even if they take over the education ministry, Mortera-Martinez argues education policy is largely devolved to Spain's regional governments.
The leader of Vox, Santiago Abascal, is hoping to double his party's seats in parliament
Since 2022, Vox has worked with the PP in a series of regional coalition governments, holding ministries such as culture and tourism. At the time FeijÃ³o had reservations about Vox joining the conservatives in government in Castilla y LeÃ³n.
The following year they went into coalition with the conservatives in Valencia, AragÃ³n, Murcia, and Extremadura, but pulled out of all five governments in 2024 when they refused to accept unaccompanied migrant children being moved to their regions.
They have since signed new coalition pacts with the PP in Extremadura, AragÃ³n, Castilla y LeÃ³n and Andalusia.
Unlike many European countries Spain has 17 autonomous communities (and two cities) that have their own parliament and their own powers. Catalonia in the north-east and the Basque Country in the north have their own police forces.
The regions matter to Sunday's result. Catalonia alone has 48 seats out of the 350 in Spain's parliament, and the Socialists have recently come to rely on regional parties for support.
SÃ¡nchez's government relied on the support of Basque separatists Bildu and two Catalan parties, ERC on the left and Junts on the right. But when Junts refused to back his housing reform, he decided to dissolve parliament.
Spain is made up of 50 constituencies which each have a minimum of two seats.
The exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla both have one, and the other 248 seats are divided proportionally according to voter numbers.
Madrid province will have 38 seats, Barcelona 32 and Valencia 16.

articles.title_orig: UK government set to publish new treaties agreed with EU
articles.title_zh: UK government set to publish new treaties agreed with EU
articles.content_orig:
The government and the EU are set to publish the texts of two treaties that were agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.
The treaties will be published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation which is designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
The BBC understands the treaties have a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.
Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch and Reform UK's Nigel Farage have suggested they would refuse to pay.
The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship.
The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.
New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected.
Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.
The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.
Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."
"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."
The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.
The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.
Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.
Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.
Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week , the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".
Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.
Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.
Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

Following a game update last week, preparing for the release of Xenoblade Chronicles 3 - Switch 2 Edition , Nintendo has now released a new overview trailer for this version of the game.
It once again goes through all the features and enhancements that will be available in the paid Switch 2 upgrade. Here's the rundown once again via the game page and official PR:
- Support for 4K resolution in TV mode (Enhanced graphics require a TV that supports 4K resolution) - Improved performance at 60 fps - New mode: Heroes' Vault - New Hero: Shimmer - Event scenes updated to be fully voiced in English and Japanese
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
In Xenoblade Chronicles 3 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition , you will join Noah and Mio, members of the opposing nations of Keves and Agnus, as they embark on a stirring journey through a war-torn world that harbors a dark secret. Master real-time RPG combat and enjoy newly voiced event scenes, enhanced 4K resolution in TV mode (with compatible television), full HD in handheld mode, and smoother, sharper gameplay at 60 frames per second.
On this adventure, you’ll command six characters, as well as a new mythical Hero called Shimmer – a speedy attacker who unleashes devastating rapid-fire combos and wields the power of Foresight to see the future. Lead your band against hordes of enemies, auto-attacking with each character’s distinct Arts and weapons. Pairs of characters can also Interlink to form a mighty Ouroboros capable of taking down the most threatening enemies with powerful Arts.

Here, with each enemy you defeat, you’ll power up a gauge you can use to enhance your abilities and gain additional allies. articles.title_orig: The Other Nvidia Romance With an Executive at a Company Linked to China
articles.title_zh: The Other Nvidia Romance With an Executive at a Company Linked to China
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A little-known figure in the palace intrigue involving Nvidia's Jensen Huang and possible chip smuggling is rapidly gaining attention. Ying Cenly Chen, a former senior executive at Super Micro Computer , is alleged to have managed a significant portion of the company's purchases of Nvidia chips during the period when Supermicro's hardware was allegedly diverted to China, according to a lawsuit. Her new company, ChronoScale, where Chen serves as CEO, has business ties to both Supermicro and Nvidia.
Chen matters because of her position at Supermicro and because of when she left. A shareholder lawsuit claims that Chen, 50, controlled Supermicro's supply of Nvidia chips and could not have been unaware of the company's alleged illicit sales. She exited Supermicro within weeks of an indictment that named Supermicro co-founder, Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw in the smuggling scheme. She is also married to Ajay "Jay" Puri, Nvidia's longtime sales chief, Chen confirmed to Fortune . Puri worked for the chipmaker for two decades before announcing his retirement in June.
That means Chen could hold some answers to the question now looming large above Nvidia, which is whether Huang, who resigned as CEO on Nov. 11, knew or turned a blind eye as its chips were potentially diverted to China. And it puts a spotlight on her role at ChronoScale, which develops datacenters that rely heavily on Nvidia chips.
Chen disputes the lawsuit's account. In emails to Fortune , she said controlling customer allocations of Nvidia chips "was not part of my job responsibility" when she worked at Supermicro. Supermicro also denied that she controlled how its supply of Nvidia GPUs were distributed.
Chen also said she agreed to join ChronoScale before the Supermicro smuggling scandal broke. She told Fortune she accepted the offer on March 10 via DocuSign , nine days before the Liaw indictment was unsealed on March 19. She said the "offer documentation was completed on April 24" and her last day at Supermicro was April 30. That timing would mean Chen remained as chief growth officer at Supermicro for seven weeks after she said she accepted the ChronoScale job, and for six weeks after the indictment.
Liaw, the Supermicro cofounder, was arrested and indicted with two others in a sweeping $2.5 billion smuggling case in March. Liaw has pleaded not guilty; one of his codefendants, Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun, has pleaded guilty. On a May 5 earnings call , days after Chen's departure, Supermicro CEO Charles Liang told analysts that "no one" at the company other than the three who had been indicted were involved in the alleged scheme. That declaration, which stunned some observers, came while the Supermicro board was still engaged in an ongoing investigation directors launched following Liaw's arrest. Under typical circumstances, Liang as CEO and co-founder who knew Liaw for three decades, wouldn't have been closely involved in an independent board-led investigation, particularly one that was ongoing at the time.
Neither Liang nor Supermicro have been named as targets in the alleged scheme, and Supermicro has said it is itself a victim and is cooperating with authorities. ChronoScale has also not been named by regulators as the target of any investigation. Puri and Nvidia declined to comment. A Supermicro spokesperson denied that Chen controlled how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers and said that after 18 years at Supermicro, Chen "voluntarily resigned in early 2026 to take the CEO role at ChronoScale."
It wasn't until August that the Supermicro board's investigation officially concluded with a finding that the investigation team "did not find any evidence that any current member of senior management had knowledge" about the alleged scheme. By that time, Chen had landed as CEO of ChronoScale, an AI cloud company based in Silicon Valley formed on May 5, 2026, when data-center developer Applied Digital merged its GPU cloud subsidiary, Applied Digital Cloud, into Ekso Bionics Holdings, a Nasdaq-listed maker of robotic exoskeletons. The combined company renamed itself ChronoScale and Applied Digital owns about 96% of it.
Now, a shareholder complaint filed in October has cast a cloud over Chen herself. In a complaint filed Oct. 9 in federal court in San Francisco, former Supermicro employees who are not named allege that Chen controlled Supermicro's supply of Nvidia chips and that she left because of the U.S. government's smuggling investigation. Chen is not a defendant in the lawsuit, she has not been charged or accused of wrongdoing by any government agency, and the allegations are unproven.
The lawsuit is a securities class action brought by investors who say Supermicro, Liang and other executives misled them about company sales and export compliance while servers were being allegedly diverted illegally to China, and that they lost money when the March indictment by federal prosecutors in Manhattan sent the stock tanking.
Chen worked at Supermicro from March 2008 to April 2026 and was most recently its chief growth officer and a senior vice president, according to ChronoScale's filings. According to Chronoscale's website, she graduated with a Bachelor's Degree in Science from Fudan University, a public university in Shanghai. The shareholder complaint describes her as a force inside Supermicro who "reported directly to" Liang and led a sales team that it says accounted for "approximately 80% of the company's total sales."
One former employee quoted in the lawsuit, described as a Supermicro sales director from July 2023 to July 2025, said Chen "had a very close relationship with Nvidia and managed the company's acquisition of GPU chips from Nvidia." Because the supply was limited and in such demand, the former employee said Nvidia "would allocate a certain number to Super Micro, and Chen decided how to distribute them among Super Micro's customers." Chen met routinely with Liang "to obtain Liang's approval of how the chips would be allocated," according to the complaint.
Supermicro disputes this allegation. "Cenly Chen did not control how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers," the spokesperson said.
A second former employee in the lawsuit, described as a sales director who worked at Supermicro until 2024, said Chen "handled all allocations of Nvidia chips to Super Micro" and had taken over responsibility for the sales team that covered China. The person said "there was no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge of the company's illicit sales."
The complaint also offers an account of why Chen left. The first former employee claimed that Chen's emails had created a potentially problematic paper trail: "It was widely known within the company that Chen had to leave because she had sent emails requesting that Nvidia release chips with serial numbers associated with the GPUs illegally diverted to customers in China." Citing the former employee, the complaint also states she "resigned so that the company could claim that no current employees were involved in the scheme for which Liaw was arrested."
Chen disputes the account.
"I do not believe this email exists, as I would never knowingly do such a thing and I don't believe I ever did," Chen told Fortune . Both former employees had left Supermicro before Chen did, according to the complaint's own description of their tenures, and it does not say how they learned the circumstances of her departure.
ChronoScale was created on May 5, when Applied Digital's cloud business merged into Ekso Bionics Holdings, a public company. Chen's hiring was not disclosed in securities filings before then. The offer letter ChronoScale filed with the SEC is dated May 5 and shows Chen's acceptance dated April 24.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine attacks Russian military base, says five planes struck
articles.title_zh: Ukraine attacks Russian military base, says five planes struck
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian forces have hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.
Ukraine struck the Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region, the General Staff said on Wednesday, adding that three MiG-31 jets were used to fire hypersonic missiles and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were damaged.
Russia did not immediately comment on the report by the General Staff, which said the Savasleyka airbase had been hit in the latest long-range attacks aimed at crippling Moscow’s war effort .
The operation followed a series of high-profile strikes by Ukrainian forces in recent days in which two Russian ships were hit in Libyan waters and a Russian vessel was struck in the Gulf of Finland .
Last week, Ukraine destroyed the road portion of Russia’s prized bridge to the Crimea peninsula after consecutive attacks.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and fighting has continued despite a renewed US-backed push to end what has become Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.
Kyiv is trying to dent Moscow’s military might as it struggles under a renewed campaign of attacks on its energy system and mounting Russian strikes on front-line cities.
Ukrainian forces are hunting Russian ballistic-missile launchers used to carry out many of those attacks, striking 16 over the past several months, Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said this week.
Renewed Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ processing volumes by 45 percent since late October, industry sources said this month. Kyiv has said it will stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow does the same.

articles.title_orig: Stocks rally in Asia, US tariffs not as dire as feared
articles.title_zh: Stocks rally in Asia, US tariffs not as dire as feared
articles.content_orig:
Asia-Pacific markets rose Thursday, tracking Wall Street gains overnight, with tech stocks rebounding from steep losses in the prior session.
Investors appear to have looked past a fresh set of U.S. tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday, targeting more than a dozen major trading partners, including China and the European Union.
South Korea's Kospi gained 1.73%, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 2.32% after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates by an expected 25 basis points, as inflation continues to run above target while a booming economy allows it room to tighten policy.
The central bank raised rates to 3.25%, a 2-year high, in its final meeting of the year, data on the Bank of Korea's website showed .
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 1.21% while the Topix edged 0.71% higher. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.15%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index rose 1.46% while mainland China's CSI 300 added 0.12%.
Asian technology stocks rebounded sharply Thursday, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
SoftBank Group surged more than 11%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 7.3%. Lasertec and Disco both gained more than 6%, while Tokyo Electron climbed 4.6%.
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 4% and 2.1%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Cryptocurrencies also traded higher, with bitcoin rising 1.58% to $60,944.60, while ether gained 1.15% to $1,702.96.
The gains come amid lingering concerns over the outlook for digital assets, with the co-founder of now-shuttered crypto exchange BitMEX Arthur Hayes telling CNBC on Tuesday that bitcoin could test $50,000 if the Nasdaq continues to slide.
Meanwhile, fresh U.S. inflation data reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.
Overnight in the U.S., the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an 1,100-point plunge on Wednesday, advancing 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to end at 50,182.95. The Nasdaq Composite , however, fell 0.62% to 23,585.80, while the S&P 500 shed 0.25% to close at 7,182.78.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday.

articles.title_orig: S. Korea's spy agency denies report about China's alleged proposal for anti-US operations
articles.title_zh: S. Korea's spy agency denies report about China's alleged proposal for anti-US operations
articles.content_orig:
Published : Nov. 26, 2026 - 10:24:22
Add The Korea Herald on Google
South Korea's spy agency has denied a media report that Beijing had proposed covert operations against the United States when the agency sought to secure the release of two informants detained by China early this year.
The Kukmin Daily reported Wednesday that China made the proposal to the National Intelligence Service for the anti-US operations, and that Washington strongly protested it, apparently leading to a chasm in the South Korea-US intelligence partnership.
"The NIS has never received any such proposal from the Chinese authorities," it said in a press notice.
The agency also said intelligence cooperation between Seoul and Washington is proceeding in a "two-way" and "mutually beneficial" manner across various fields, including counterintelligence.
Concerns about bilateral intelligence collaboration have continued following reports earlier this year that the US partially limited Seoul's access to its satellite-based intelligence on North Korea after Unification Minister Chung Dong-young referred to the North's Kusong area as one of the uranium enrichment sites.
Seoul believes that Chung's reference to the Kusong site is based on "open-source" information, while the US side regards it as a disclosure of confidential US information.
Commenting on intelligence cooperation between Seoul and Washington, a senior US official told Yonhap News Agency last month that the US expects South Korea to "uphold the standards of our decadeslong alliance, in particular concerning matters of intelligence and counterintelligence."
Meanwhile, a South Korean engineer, who previously worked for a Korean firm, has been detained in China for nearly three years following his arrest on espionage charges in December 2023, according to a government source. The person has been suspected of informing the NIS of suspected leaks of South Korean semiconductor technology.
The NIS is believed to have started earnest efforts for the detainee's release after President Lee Jae Myung's administration took office last year.
The agency is said to have even considered negotiating a "swap deal" in the first half of this year, offering information on an illegal intelligence agent, known as a "black" operative, in exchange for its citizen's release. The black operative was reportedly affiliated with a third country, not the US or Japan. (Yonhap)

articles.title_orig: Billions in Data Center Deals Grind to Halt After AI Chip Curbs
articles.title_zh: Billions in Data Center Deals Grind to Halt After AI Chip Curbs
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.title_orig: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 25, 2026
articles.title_zh: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 25, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
There are two apparently contradictory trends right now in the Russia-Ukraine war. There is an unmistakable escalation, from Ukrainian strikes on Russian vessels as far apart as Finland and Libya, to Moscow’s missiles crashing down in a NATO ally.
But there is also a renewed sense of urgency in the push for peace, with U.S. officials saying Russia has accepted a form of Article 5-style security guarantee for Ukraine, and talk of a deal as soon as January 2027. Talks in Abu Dhabi are expected to continue.
These diverging forces may be cause and effect. The nearer a settlement appears, the stronger each side's incentive to improve its hand before the bargaining stops, fueling an intensification of offensive activity.
As Italy's foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, observed on Monday , once peace talks begin, "there is always an increase in military activity." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was clear that Ukraine is haggling over a price for peace that may come sooner than later.
He said the Americans are pushing for a peace deal before January, when a new Democratic-majority Congress takes control after they routed Trump’s Republicans in the midterm elections.
“There’s a desire to move very quickly, both we and the Russians understand that,” Zelensky told Bloomberg . “We understand what the price might be. We very much want peace too, but not at Ukraine’s expense alone.”
Escalation can create the conditions for peace. But brinkmanship works only when everyone can see the brink. From the Baltic to Benghazi, it is getting harder to find. Can peace come before escalation escapes all control?
On Friday, three Russian cruise missiles came down in southeastern Poland, a NATO ally that borders Ukraine. One is believed to have landed about 22 miles from where European troops were holding an unprecedented exercise for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
They were, in effect, rehearsing for the peace. Donald Tusk, Poland's prime minister, said it looked like "an intentional provocation."
The day before, Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping had issued a "Declaration toward Peace" in Shenzhen, China, which did not mention Ukraine, though the leaders committed to "maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Later that day, Putin, vowing revenge for Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge, ruled out any moratorium on attacks on energy infrastructure or in the Black Sea. Since then, Ukraine has faced more massive, deadly aerial strikes, including on the capital Kyiv.
This weekend, things escalated further. On Saturday, Ukrainian drones set a military-linked Russian cargo ship ablaze in international waters. It drifted into Finland's, where Finnish, Estonian as well as Russian crews helped fight the fire.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," said Petteri Orpo , Finland's prime minister, before affirming Ukraine's right to “fight back against the aggressor.”
Then, on Sunday, Ukrainian sea drones left the Merkury , one of Russia's newest corvettes, capsized at its berth in Benghazi, Libya, some 1,500 miles from the front line in a stunning attack. The message was clear: Russian hardware is safe nowhere.
So much for stability and security. Events are following their own dangerous and disordered path.
Yet Trump says there is still a "real good chance" of a deal on Ukraine, and soon. His son-in-law and envoy, Jared Kushner, believes Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-style security guarantees for postwar Ukraine. There is greater European engagement with Russia, too.
Korea is the classic precedent. Armistice talks began in July 1951 and ran for two years and 17 days. Fighting still continued throughout. About 45 percent of America's casualties in the war came as negotiators talked. The armistice line was simply where the armies stood.
A similar logic may be at work now. Hunting Russian ships from the Baltic to the Mediterranean raises Moscow's cost of continuing the war, which Kyiv hopes to convert into leverage at the table. Whether it can is another matter.
Zelensky now calls Russian-flagged ships, and anything carrying weapons or sanctioned cargo, legitimate targets in Russian or neutral waters, a broader test than the law of naval warfare usually allows.
Russia, meanwhile, is once again pounding Ukraine's power grid as winter months begin to bite, intending to increase the pressure on the population. The U.N. says attacks on energy infrastructure are more extensive and systematic than a year ago.
The situation is plainly worsening, yet neither side is emerging as the winner.
I. William Zartman , an American scholar of negotiation, argued that wars ripen for settlement when both sides feel trapped in a mutually hurting stalemate, see a way out and, ideally, glimpse catastrophe ahead.
"The ripe moment becomes the godchild of brinkmanship," Zartman wrote. In 1962, a glimpse of the nuclear abyss over Cuba produced a swift bargain : Soviet missiles out of Cuba, American ones quietly out of Turkey.
But Zartman also warned that pain can stiffen resistance rather than soften it, and conceded that his theory explains why talks open, not how they close.
The Ukraine war's talks have opened once again. But closing them is the hard part. More so when Russia refuses a ceasefire as a condition for peace talks. And some of its officials are already rejecting the terms Americans are floating as tentatively agreed.
A day after Kushner spoke, Sergei Ryabkov, Russia's deputy foreign minister, called any "quasi membership" of NATO for Ukraine totally unacceptable. Trump waved the contradiction away as negotiating theater.
The last round, in Abu Dhabi, produced another large prisoner-exchange deal but no breakthrough, and the Kremlin says no date is set for the next, though both sides remain open to further talks.
That leaves the darker precedent of 1914, when a local war became a global one through alliances and miscalculation.
This war now reaches into divided Libya. The Merkury had docked under a deal with the eastern government while, Libyan officials say, Ukrainian drone teams operate from the west.
Musa al-Koni, a deputy head of Libya's Presidential Council, even likened the strikes to a declaration of war on Libya. Kyiv, increasingly unbounded by geographical constraints, real or imagined, calls them lawful self-defense under the U.N. Charter.
Perhaps the biggest risk of escalation, though, is in Russia’s relentless testing of European NATO allies through its grey-zone campaign of hybrid warfare. One misjudgment, one overreaction, one misread action and NATO’s Article 5 is in play.
If allies judged one of them to be the victim of an armed attack—perhaps even the recent missiles landing in Poland—then America, too, would be bound to take "such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force."
Britain's chief of defense intelligence, Lieutenant General Matthew Jones, thinks that Russia does not actively seek war with NATO. "However, my greatest fear is the risk of a significant miscalculation," he said .
Resolving the war in Ukraine, and perhaps with it coming to a grand European security bargain with Russia, would massively reduce the risk of such a miscalculation befalling us all.
Perhaps that will happen soon, maybe even in early 2027 if all the escalation is, paradoxically, in the service of making peace.
But there is another possibility, as in Korea: years of talking while the death and fighting thunder on in the background, at risk of sparking something much bigger.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu says corruption trial ‘must end’ as court suggests dropping case
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu says corruption trial ‘must end’ as court suggests dropping case
articles.content_orig:
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for an immediate end to his long-running corruption trial after judges cast doubt on the charges and recommended dropping a case in which he is accused of bribery.
Netanyahu on Wednesday said the “fabricated cases” against him were falling apart, in a televised statement at the Israeli parliament.
Meanwhile, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s parliamentary bloc voted in favour of conducting an independent investigation into the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
The judges’ recommendations came as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival after inconclusive October 27 elections.
Eisenkot, who is Netanyahu’s main rival, has been tasked with forming a government, and if Netanyahu is no longer prime minister, he would lose his leverage to avoid a potential jail sentence.
“Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family,” Netanyahu said in his speech.
“Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul. Who will give those years back to us?”
“The trial must end immediately,” he added.
During a hearing in Jerusalem on Wednesday regarding three corruption cases against Netanyahu, judges recommended dropping one, reconsidering another and suggested resolving the third through an agreement, Israeli media reported.
In Case 4000, in which Netanyahu is accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, judges indicated there was little chance of a conviction.
That case is considered to be the most serious Netanyahu faces and involves him allegedly offering regulatory favours for a telecoms company in exchange for favourable media coverage.
Netanyahu is alleged to have negotiated with Shaul Elovitch, the controlling shareholder of Israeli telecommunications giant Bezeq, to get positive coverage on his Walla news site in exchange for policies benefitting Bezeq.
On Wednesday, Israeli media reported Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman saying that proving the bribery charge in that case faced “considerable difficulties”.
Netanyahu, who has been in power on and off for three decades, has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and denounced the cases as a politically motivated plot against him.
He is the first sitting Israeli prime minister to stand trial.
Israel’s Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who was unusually summoned to the hearing on Wednesday, said she would consider the judges’ recommendations and was ready for either a verdict or a plea deal.
In Case 2000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over an alleged deal with the owner of Yediot Aharonot for favourable coverage in exchange for curbs on rival newspaper Israel Hayom. Judges on Wednesday questioned whether his actions constituted a crime and recommended reconsidering the case.
In Case 1000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over allegedly accepting luxury gifts from wealthy individuals in exchange for favours. Judges recommended reaching an agreement to conclude the case.
Netanyahu’s right-wing allies cheered the court’s recommendations and demanded the trial be brought to an end.
“After years of persecution against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the time has come to put an end to a trial that was flawed from the outset,” Israel Katz, who is the defence minister in Netanyahu’s caretaker government, wrote on X.
Netanyahu’s corruption trial opened in May 2020.
During his most recent term, which started in late 2022, Netanyahu proposed far-reaching judicial reforms that critics say sought to weaken the courts.
With coalition negotiations under way, Eisenkot’s camp is already trying to start unravelling some of the Netanyahu-era judicial reforms in parliament.
The presidential contender is expected to meet Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday evening.
His centrist Yashar party said a day earlier that it had agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.
Lieberman has ruled out forming a coalition with Arab-led parties that could hand them a majority in parliament. That has frustrated Democrats chief Yair Golan, who has been pushing Eisenkot to reach a deal with parties representing Israel’s 21 percent Arab minority to make good on his campaign promise to bring down Netanyahu.
The Israeli parliament’s preliminary approval on Wednesday of a probe into the country’s failures prior to the October 7 attack dealt a blow to Netanyahu, who has repeatedly opposed the move.
The vote was the first of four needed ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠to pass a law establishing a state commission to investigate the Hamas attack.
The parliament also voted in favour of a bill seeking to impose term limits on prime ministers and restrict them from serving while under criminal indictment, seemingly taking aim at Netanyahu.
Eisenkot also faced a new challenge on Tuesday after the left-wing Democrats suspended coalition talks, further complicating his potential path to power.
The Yashar party leader has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.

articles.title_orig: Xi unleashes China ‘earthquake’ with shock ouster of rising star
articles.title_zh: Xi unleashes China ‘earthquake’ with shock ouster of rising star
articles.content_orig:
He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials. But now Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s influential politburo, appears to be the latest senior official brought down by President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge.
The hammer unexpectedly came down on Chen in the form of a two-line bulletin on the Xinhua news agency Tuesday: He is “suspected of serious violations of Party discipline and law and is currently under disciplinary review and supervisory investigation” — a common euphemism for corruption crackdowns on ruling Communist Party officials under Xi.
Public announcements such as these usually mark the end of a political career in China. Chen has made no public statement.
He is the fourth politburo member to be purged in less than two years, part of a broader crackdown that has swept aside top military leaders as Xi consolidates power. He is set to extend his rule next year, at a party congress that is held once every five years and looms over the preceding months.
But Chen’s abrupt downfall took many close observers of China by surprise, given his profile and career path would usually point to a bright future.
“He was potentially going to the highest level, which would be the standing committee. And I think from a lot of Western observers, people thought he had even better prospects,” Damien Ma, the Singapore-based director of the Carnegie China think tank, told NBC News.
Some analysts have speculated that Xi, increasingly viewed as likely to rule for life, may have been purging a viable replacement. Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said however that Chen was “someone who could rise further but not as a successor.”
Chen, a 62-year-old technocrat known as a friend of foreign business and an advocate for AI, was an environmental scientist who studied in London and swiftly rose through the party’s ranks. He served as China’s environmental minister, Beijing’s mayor and the party secretary in Shanghai — a post once held by Xi and widely considered a stepping stone to bigger things.
Just last month, Chen hosted Apple Chairman Tim Cook, welcoming the U.S. tech giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths” and bring more products to the city, a financial and cultural hub that has long served as a connection between China and the international community.
In his last public appearance last week, during a tour of a shipping facility, Chen called for advancing the industry’s digital transformation.
By Wednesday, Chen’s name has been removed from some official websites. A webpage on the Shanghai government site showing that meeting with Cook is now showing a 404 message, or not found.
Chen is just the latest senior official in the crosshairs of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign and emphasis on party discipline, which analysts say is as much about loyalty as it is about reform.
“It is a warning to all technocrats, as Chen was a rising star among technocrats and had no apparent failures in a technocratic way. So, message is: adhere to strict party discipline and demonstrate unquestionable loyalty to Xi or else,” Tsang said.
The party’s Central Committee, which has about 200 mostly male leaders, vowed to “ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive” at its closed-door gathering, the fifth plenum, last month.
“What they’ve been building as part of this discipline machine over the last 15 years is to kind of implement their sort of internal operating system of how they deal with, let’s say, bad eggs within the party,” Ma, of Carnegie China, said.
“The top leadership is normalizing this anti-corruption, this self-cleansing,” Ma said. “It is now a normal part of what the party expects, and they’re trying to embed that over time and down to every single level,” he added.
The Chinese government has not announced any charges against Chen, who was the youngest member of the country’s elite decision-making body. The 24-member Politburo was unveiled in 2022 but is now down to 21 members after the purges. Last month, top general Zhang Shengmin was elevated to the body in a rare addition.
Chen’s undoing comes a year before the party’s top leadership is reshuffled at the 21st Communist Party Congress, when Xi is expected to solidify control even further and cement another five-year term at the helm of the country.
Born in 1964, Chen studied at the prestigious Tsinghua university, long a major pipeline for senior party officials and where he served as president from 2012 to 2015. His name has now been removed from Tsinghua’s online list of former presidents.
After studying at Tsinghua in the 1980s, he moved for a decade to Britain, where he obtained a doctorate from Imperial College London in 1993.
Chen returned to Tsinghua’s environmental science and engineering department in 1998 before being named the university’s president in 2012, according to an official biography .
He’s authored dozens of papers, including on carbon emission reduction and water quality monitoring .
The relatively young Chen would ride around campus on his bike and built a reputation for pushing institutional reforms in his three years at the helm of the university, according to an article in People’s Digest , a magazine affiliated with the People’s Daily, the community party’s official newspaper.
The article, titled “From University President to Cabinet Minister,” was published in 2015, the same year he was picked to lead the Environmental Protection Ministry. In 2017, Chen became mayor of the capital, Beijing, where he oversaw the 2022 Winter Olympics during the Covid pandemic.
Later that year he was transferred to Shanghai and became the party chief, a coveted role that Xi took on himself in 2007 before becoming the country’s leader in 2013.
There, he became heavily involved with the tech industry, regularly hosting CEOs and advocating for more investment into Shanghai, where the World AI Conference was hosted earlier this year.
Chen hosted Elon Musk in 2023 to discuss Tesla’s operations in the city. Last year, he accompanied Xi to an AI hub there. And last month, Chen met with several European tech leaders, in addition to hosting Cook.
Alongside the top post in Shanghai, Chen also was elected for a five-year term as a member of the Politburo, China’s elite decision-making body headed by Xi.
While the Politburo is not the absolute apex of power, he was seen as a contender the much-smaller Politburo’s Standing Committee, which is made up of the country’s highest ranking officials.
“If you’re party secretary of one of the four big municipalities, Beijing, Shanghai, Chongqing and Tianjin, you have pretty good prospects. That’s sort of an indication that you’re on your way up,” Ma said.
Whether or not Chen’s ousting deals a blow to the country’s technology ambitions and its race for dominance in artificial intelligence, remains to be seen, Ma said. But either way, his downfall will force a rethink among those seeking to predict the route to power in modern China.
“Part of it is thinking through what is really the new criteria to get to the top, and they may not be what we thought just a few months ago,” Ma added.
Max Burman is deputy editor in the London bureau of NBC News Digital.
