articles.title_orig: Magyar meets Zelenskyy: Hungary and Ukraine make a fresh start after the icy relations of the Orban era
articles.title_zh: Magyar meets Zelenskyy: Hungary and Ukraine make a fresh start after the icy relations of the Orban era
articles.content_orig:
The location and the gesture were carefully chosen: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood side by side, laid flowers and bowed their heads at the military cemetery in the center of the Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod.
One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine .
Magyar intentionally chose not to begin his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister at a government building. Instead, his Tuesday afternoon visit began at a place where he could demonstrate his solidarity with Ukraine more clearly than anywhere else.
Uzhhorod, known as Ungvar in Hungarian, is the capital of Ukraine's Transcarpathia region, which is home to around 80,000 members of Ukraine's Hungarian minority. Thousands of ethnic Hungarians are fighting Russian occupying forces on the front lines.
For Hungary , where ethnic Hungarian minorities in neighboring countries traditionally play an important role, the war is therefore closer to home than it is for other European countries.
Magyar described his visit to Ukraine as a "historic day" in a Facebook post. Before the ceremony at the cemetery in Uzhhorod, he said: "I bring with me the solidarity of the Hungarian people. We stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."
Zelenskyy responded on X, saying "We appreciate this gesture of respect toward those who sacrificed their lives for Ukraine's independence."
The meeting between Magyar and Zelenskyy marked a turning point in Hungary's approach to Ukraine.
The two leaders repeatedly shook hands throughout the day. Such scenes would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. The propaganda of Magyar's pro-Russian predecessor, Viktor Orban , portrayed Ukraine as a "mafia state" and "lawless country" on an almost daily basis.
Under Orban, relations between Hungary and Ukraine reached a historic low .
Now the two countries are seeking a political reset, which is important not only for Hungary and Ukraine but for Europe as a whole. After all, Orban's repeated obstruction of support for Ukraine drove the EU to the brink of despair.
During talks in Uzhhorod, the two leaders also agreed to closer economic cooperation.
The talks centered on Hungarian diesel supplies to Ukraine, greater use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies, and joint infrastructure projects, including the opening of new border crossings and a direct rail link between Budapest and Kyiv.
Nevertheless, no formal agreements were signed on Tuesday.
At a subsequent news conference, journalists asked questions about sensitive issues between the two countries: minority rights, Ukraine's EU integration and a new EU loan for Ukraine.
Throughout the day, the two men were visibly keen to avoid any discord.
Magyar, for example, described his angry outburst over Ukraine's "Carpathian Eight" initiative in parliament in late September as a "misunderstanding" and suggested that Hungary might, after all, take part.
Zelenskyy's cautious replies to journalists suggest that he knows his country's path to EU membership also runs through Budapest.
One of Magyar's statements on Tuesday was key: "We've finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation."
Even before taking office in early May 2026, Magyar had promised to reset relations with Ukraine. But the process has not been entirely smooth.
In many respects — but certainly not all — Magyar is distancing himself from his predecessor. He has made no bones of the fact that he sees Russia as the aggressor, but he rejects both arms deliveries to Ukraine and even the transit of weapons across Hungarian territory.
Magyar previously accused Ukraine of treating ethnic Hungarians as second-class citizens — a claim that is not borne out by the facts. He pressed for greater minority rights and for a time blocked the opening of negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks.
Magyar also departed from diplomatic convention by choosing the location of his meeting with Zelenskyy in Ukraine: Indeed, it was Magyar who invited Zelenskyy to Transcarpathia.
Magyar's sometimes confrontational tone toward Ukraine can also be explained by the need to avoid appearing too pro-Ukrainian to the Hungarian public.
According to a November 2026 poll conducted by the think tank Globsec , 33% of Hungarians would now support their country providing military aid to Ukraine. Although this is much more than during Orban's time in office, many Hungarians remain skeptical of Ukraine.
That's why Olena Halushka, a Ukrainian political scientist at the International Centre for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV), sees some aspects of Magyar's visit as a concession to public opinion in Hungary.
"Magyar has taken over a deeply polarized country," she told DW's Ukrainian Service. "A visit to Transcarpathia is more of a step for the Hungarian population than for Ukraine."
Ukraine accommodated not only Magyar's choice of location but also Hungary's demands for better protection of minority rights, which were set out in a 10-point plan in June. That's because EU integration is one of the country's top political priorities.
After planned restrictions on the use of minority languages were withdrawn in late 2023, Ukraine's parliament in early October passed a law on minority language rights that in some respects goes even further than European standards.
Hungary subsequently dropped its obstruction of the opening of negotiating clusters for Ukraine's EU accession.
Laszlo Zubanics, chairman of the Hungarian Democratic Federation in Ukraine (UMDSZ, one of two Hungarian political parties in Transcarpathia), told DW that the Magyar-Zelenskyy meeting was "historic."
He particularly welcomed the fact that Ukraine will probably implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights "not only by the end of 2027, but much sooner, within just a few months."
A Hungarian diplomat who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity also called the meeting "historic," adding that after the Orban government's anti-Ukrainian policies, trust now needs to be rebuilt, and that personal meetings between the two leaders play an important role in that process.
The diplomat went on to say that Hungary not only wants to ensure that the rights of the Hungarian minority are protected, it also has a strong interest in being involved in Ukraine's reconstruction.
Overall, the diplomat concluded, both sides are very keen to expand economic cooperation.
Hungarian political scientist Daniel Hegedus of the Institute for European Politics ( IEP ) in Berlin told DW that while the meeting was a "symbolic milestone," it will be important to see "how the two political leaders capitalize on the symbolic political capital generated by this meeting."
No observers have suggested that this is the grand finale of reconciliation between Hungary and Ukraine.
Nevertheless, Tuesday's reset sends an important signal to Europe, namely that if the political will is there, a deep gulf that has existed for years can be transformed into a set of diverging interests that can be addressed through negotiations.
Or, as Zelenskyy put it, now there are "all the opportunities to build hopefully constructive relations."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title_orig: Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
articles.title_zh: Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
articles.content_orig:
After eight years of Socialist-led government under Pedro Sánchez, Spain is at a crossroads.
Snap elections are taking place on Sunday 29 November, and voters face a choice of continued left-wing rule or a conservative-led government, with the likely support of far-right Vox.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo's conservative People's Party is narrowly ahead of the Socialist PSOE in most polls.
He has spoken of Spain being probably at "the most significant moment in our country for the past 50 years", and he aims to "repair the state, regenerate democracy, reunited the nation and recover Spain's ambition and self-esteem". But it is unlikely he could do anything without the backing of Vox, who are third in the opinion polls.
For more on Feijóo and who else to watch in this election - read here .
Spain has a population of almost 50 million, and almost 39 million people have the right to vote for the Congress and the upper house, the Senate. The polls open at 09:00 (08:00 GMT) on Sunday and close at 20:00 (19:00 GMT), when the first exit polls come out.
Sánchez called this vote eight months early after MPs rejected planned changes to Spain's housing laws.
He was responding to nationwide protests after an 87-year-old woman called Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her rented flat in Madrid and later died.
But his government lost the support of a centre-right party called Junts from the north-eastern region of Catalonia which sought to protect the rights of property owners.
Housing remains one of the hot-button issues for voters, but they are also focused on the high cost of living, corruption and immigration. And the election takes place within weeks of a devastating rail disaster that has shattered confidence in Spain’s high-speed rail network.
Spain's property prices and rents have soared by more than 80% from 2015 to 2025, and wages have not kept pace.
Spain has a combination of high demand and scarce supply: the Bank of Spain estimates 700,000 homes are needed to ease the pressure.
The result is that millions of Spaniards have little chance to buy a house, while they live in fear of eviction if their rent is increased. On 11 November, four million Spaniards were galvanised into joining the first general strike since 2012, according to the unions.
Pedro Sánchez has embraced housing reform as a big campaign issue and left-wing parties have promised rent controls and protection against eviction, while the right is focusing on building more homes, tax breaks for homebuyers and planning deregulation.
Support for the Socialists is down from 2023, but even then he came second in the race and relied on the backing of other parties, mainly on the left, to stay in power. This time those other left-wing parties, in particular the Broad Front (Frente Amplio) have fallen back and the big questions now are more about Feijóo's conservatives.
"It is a demobilisation of the left. Sanchez's party is not doing well," says Jacobo Ramos Folch, Policy Analyst and visiting professor at the University of Navarra.
"That lack of majority is really a reality – and the rise of Vox. What is changing that shift of majorities is the rise of Vox."
Vox have been around since 2013 but polls suggest this time they could almost double their 33 seats in Spain's lower house, the Congress.
Their big themes are "national priority" – putting Spanish citizens first for subsidies and welfare, along with repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain.
Migration has become a key challenge for Spain, and Alberto Nuñez Feijoo has accused his rival of being a "problem for Europe when it comes to immigration" after the influx of tens of thousands of migrants into the exclave of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco in July.
This month too, the Canary Island of El Hierro has seen record arrivals, with 2,000 people landing there on 24 November. Abascal has spoken of "another invasion".
And yet a recent CIS survey put it far behind housing, cost of living, healthcare and working conditions.
The PP and Vox have bitterly criticised the Socialist-led government for a drive to legalise unauthorised migrants this year that attracted 1.2 million applications.
Feijóo's party wants to see more controlled immigration. Vox has called for mass deportations.
Feijóo has accused the Socialists of being "the most corrupt party" that Spain has ever seen, and a number of cases have involved Sánchez's inner circle and family.
People should distinguish between real and "fictitious" corruption allegations, says el momento más trascendental.
His former transport minister José Luis Ábalos has been given 24 years in prison over multiple corruption offences.
Leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.
Sánchez's wife Begoña Gómez faces trial for alleged misuse of public funds and using her marriage to further her academic career. She denies wrongdoing. And his brother David Sánchez has been banned from public office for nine years for administrative misconduct.
Feijóo has made clear his objective is to form a majority and make "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox. As far as a coalition is concerned, he says he will respect the will of Spanish voters, but maintains Abascal has never talked to him about running any ministries.
The PP leader is clear that Vox's national priority policy would run counter to Spain's constitution and European Union treaties: "No-one can sign illegal agreements."
Even if they were to go into coalition, Camino Mortera-Martinez of the Centre for European Reform, and a former European affairs adviser to the Spanish prime minister is not convinced Vox would wield much influence.
"They're not going to get any of the core ministries. They're not going to get defence or home affairs or foreign policy or economy," she told the BBC. Even if they take over the education ministry, Mortera-Martinez argues education policy is largely devolved to Spain's regional governments.
Since 2022, Vox has worked with the PP in a series of regional coalition governments, holding ministries such as culture and tourism. At the time Feijóo had reservations about Vox joining the conservatives in government in Castilla y León.
The following year they went into coalition with the conservatives in Valencia, Aragón, Murcia, and Extremadura, but pulled out of all five governments in 2024 when they refused to accept unaccompanied migrant children being moved to their regions.
They have since signed new coalition pacts with the PP in Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León and Andalusia.
Unlike many European countries Spain has 17 autonomous communities (and two cities) that have their own parliament and their own powers. Catalonia in the north-east and the Basque Country in the north have their own police forces.
The regions matter to Sunday's result. Catalonia alone has 48 seats out of the 350 in Spain's parliament, and the Socialists have recently come to rely on regional parties for support.
Sánchez's government relied on the support of Basque separatists Bildu and two Catalan parties, ERC on the left and Junts on the right. But when Junts refused to back his housing reform, he decided to dissolve parliament.
Spain is made up of 50 constituencies which each have a minimum of two seats.
The exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla both have one, and the other 248 seats are divided proportionally according to voter numbers.
Madrid province will have 38 seats, Barcelona 32 and Valencia 16.
To win a seat, a party has to win 3% of the vote in a province, but in smaller provinces with fewer seats parties generally need more than that.

articles.title_orig: South Korea's Kospi leads gains as tech rebound lifts Asia markets
articles.title_zh: South Korea's Kospi leads gains as tech rebound lifts Asia markets
articles.content_orig:
Asia-Pacific markets rose Thursday, tracking Wall Street gains overnight, with tech stocks rebounding from steep losses in the prior session.
South Korea's Kospi gained 1.73%, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 2.32% after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates by an expected 25 basis points, as inflation continues to run above target while a booming economy allows it room to tighten policy.
The central bank raised rates to 3.25%, a 2-year high, in its final meeting of the year, data on the Bank of Korea's website showed .
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 1.21% in early trade, while the Topix edged 0.71% higher. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.15%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index rose 1.46% while mainland China's CSI 300 added 0.12%.
Asian technology stocks rebounded sharply Thursday, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
SoftBank Group surged more than 11%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 7.3%. Lasertec and Disco both gained more than 6%, while Tokyo Electron climbed 4.6%.
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 4% and 2.1%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Investors appears to have looked past a fresh set of U.S. tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday, targeting more than a dozen major trading partners, including China and the European Union.
Meanwhile, fresh U.S. inflation data reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.
Overnight in the U.S., the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an 1,100-point plunge on Wednesday, advancing 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to end at 50,182.95. The Nasdaq Composite , however, fell 0.62% to 23,585.80, while the S&P 500 shed 0.25% to close at 7,182.78.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday.

articles.title_orig: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
articles.title_zh: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
articles.content_orig:
An artist's rendering of SpaceX's Starmind spacecraft in orbit around the Earth. Graphic: SpaceX
About a year after Elon Musk began musing about the anticipated benefits of shifting data center operations from the ground to space, the Federal Communications Commission granted approval to SpaceX to do just that.
In an order published the day before Thanksgiving, the FCC authorized SpaceX to proceed with its plans to construct and operate a mega constellation of up to 1 million satellites called ‘Starmind’. SpaceX filed its petition for this constellation back on Jan. 30, 2026.
The order requires SpaceX to deploy the first of these satellites by Nov. 25, 2033. During a talk hosted by Baron Capital, SpaceX founder Elon Musk said that he anticipates the first of these spacecraft launching in the third quarter of 2027.
SpaceX is manufacturing the Stamind spacecraft in partnership with Nvidia.
“We’ll start off slow, but then it will ramp to significant volume probably in ’28 and then very large volume in ’29,” Musk said.
According to the FCC’s order, SpaceX will need to have 50 percent of the Starmind constellation deployed by Nov. 25, 2038, and the full constellation by Nov. 25, 2040.
For comparison, SpaceX currently operates a constellation of Starlink satellites that consist of nearly 11,200 spacecraft in orbit, according to the latest stats maintained by respected orbital tracker and astronomer, Dr. Jonathan McDowell.
“Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in [artificial intelligence],” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr in a press release. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment.”
In a reply to the announcement on his social media site, X, Musk thanked Carr and stated, “Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”
In its order, the FCC said that these satellites would be deployed “into orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.”
As described on its website, SpaceX said each of these satellites would have a wingspan of 75 meters (246 ft) and a deployed height of 30 meters (98 ft). During a talk about orbital safety at the International Astronautical Congress in October, Michael Nicholls, the senior vice president of Starlink and AI at SpaceX, described the way that these satellites will need to operate in relation to one another to provide the desired computing capability to those back on Earth.
“We believe that we need to operate clusters of satellites in tight formation to get enough coherent compute together, such that we can run these AI models efficiently,” Nicholls said. “Every one of these satellites might be something like a 250 kilowatt satellite, or roughly a rack of compute in space, something like a NVL 72, if you’re familiar with that. But the cluster of satellites will be 10-ish satellites that’s interconnected with 10 terabits or so of bandwidth between them, and then interconnected into the broader constellation and into Starlink.”
In the FCC order, the agency stated the Starmind constellation will communicate over optical links. However, it was also granted the ability to use Ka-band frequencies in the 18.8-19.3 GHz (space-to-Earth) and 28.6-29.1 GHz (Earth-to-space) for telemetry, tracking and command (TT&C) use “only in the event its optical links experience a failure.”
The agency said SpaceX’s plan to only use those Ka-band frequencies in that limited use sufficiently addresses concerns submitted by Viasat, Amazon Leo, the American Astronomical Society and others regarding potential radiofrequency interference. In issuing its order, the FCC also rejected petitions to deny that came from those three and others.
In response to Wednesday’s ruling, the AAS said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the decision and called the constellation “at odds with a spirit of cooperation and goodwill.”
“The AAS is gravely concerned about the future of federally funded astronomical research under such a fundamentally altered night sky, and the resulting waste of taxpayer dollars invested in astronomical facilities throughout the country and the world,” the AAS said in part. “While we hope that SpaceX will continue to coordinate with the National Science Foundation, we remain concerned by the lack of formal coordination requirements in the license granted to SpaceX in this case.
“We believe that it is critical for the FCC to consider the protection of optical and infrared astronomy when assessing applications from satellite operators, in the absence of another licensing agency that can take these concerns into account.”
The FCC argued in its order that concerns related to optical astronomy were “sufficiently addressed in SpaceX’s application and supplemental material” and added that it would not need to further address the AAS’ concerns since they are “regarding potential non-spectrum related impacts” that are “outside the scope of the [orbital data centers] radiofrequency operations.”
In addressing concerns about orbital debris mitigation, the FCC noted that “SpaceX will deploy its satellites at lower altitudes in order to test them post deployment to ensure they are working before moving to higher altitudes associated with longer in-orbit durations, and it observes that the Starmind satellite propulsion systems will allow for orbit raising, station-keeping, and transit for disposal while still performing conjunction risk mitigation maneuvers.”
Nicholls addressed this in his October talk as well, arguing that the sheer size of the proposed Starmind constellation will require “significantly” more reliability.
“We need to figure out proximity ops, how to operate these satellites together in close formation. We need to think about the sources of debris like micrometeoroids and make sure that we do not accumulate debris. And then we need to think about satellite end of life,” Nicholls said.
“As an example for end of life, it may make sense that for Starmind we may not want to re-enter satellites into the Earth’s atmosphere. We may want to keep them out of Earth orbit into heliocentric orbits or graveyard orbits, and this will be new conops that we have not had to design for in the past.”
The FCC order said that it deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites into heliocentric orbits. This would affect satellites in operation above 600 km in altitude.
“Because SpaceX has not provided sufficient information for the Commission to determine whether its alternative disposal methods are compliant with the Commission’s requirements, SpaceX’s waiver request is deferred. Prior to deploying and operating any Starmind satellites that will not be disposed via atmospheric re-entry, SpaceX must file an application for modification of this authorization and provide sufficient justification for any requested waiver(s) of the Commission’s rules.”
Like with its Starlink Version 3 satellites, SpaceX would deploy its Starmind satellites using its Starship-Super Heavy rockets. The company recently completed its second orbital flight with the launcher and has deployed a total of 52 Starlink V3 satellites from Starship.
SpaceX said it will manufacture its Starmind satellites at its facilities in Bastrop, Texas, located about 350 miles north of Starbase, Texas, from which the rockets launch.

articles.title_orig: Russia has passed the biggest military budget since Soviet times
articles.title_zh: Russia has passed the biggest military budget since Soviet times
articles.content_orig:
Russia’s State Duma has passed the third reading of a federal budget bill for 2027–2029 that allocates over 50 trillion rubles (approximately $609 billion) to defense, according to the Russian parliament’s official television channel, Duma TV , as reported by Militarnyi .
Under the State Duma Defense Committee’s conclusion on draft law No. 615-9, Russia plans to spend 17.15 trillion rubles ($208.8 billion) on defense in 2027, marking an increase of roughly one-third compared to the 12.93 trillion rubles ($157.4 billion) allocated for 2026 in the previous budget plan.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over the next three years, total funding for national defense will reach 50.05 trillion rubles ($609.3 billion). Specifically, Moscow plans to allocate 17.15 trillion rubles ($208.8 billion, or 6.91% of GDP) in 2027, 16.61 trillion rubles ($202.2 billion, or 6.3% of GDP) in 2028, and 16.30 trillion rubles ($198.4 billion, or 5.79% of GDP) in 2029. These figures include both public and classified budget expenditures under the “National Defense” category.
Compared to the previous three-year budget plan, defense funding has been increased by 3.58 trillion rubles ($43.6 billion) for 2027 and by 3.56 trillion rubles ($43.3 billion) for 2028.
Overall, total spending for Russia’s federal budget in 2027 is set at 48.74 trillion rubles ($593.3 billion). Direct spending on national defense will account for roughly 35.2% of all federal expenditures, not including additional funding for security and law enforcement agencies listed under other budget sections.
In total, national defense spending in the 2027–2029 budget exceeds the previous three-year budget plan by approximately 10.5 trillion rubles ($127.8 billion).
According to The Moscow Times , this surge in military expenditures will be accompanied by funding cuts across several civilian sectors. Compared to the 2026 figures outlined in the prior budget plan, spending on the national economy will drop by roughly 3%, housing and communal services by 8%, healthcare by 3%, and social policy by 6%.
Russia’s federal budget deficit for 2027 is projected at 5.44 trillion rubles ($66.2 billion), or 2.2% of GDP, with government borrowing expected to serve as the primary source for covering the shortfall.
Previously, it was reported that Russia’s Central Bank has been selling gold from its reserves for ten consecutive months to help cover a widening federal budget deficit, projected to reach 7.3 trillion rubles ($81.1 billion) this year, twice the amount initially anticipated.
The latest reduction brought the country’s total gold reserves to 72.8 million ounces, their lowest level since late 2019.
The State Duma is the lower house of Russia's parliament, the Federal Assembly, responsible for drafting and passing federal laws along with approving certain government appointments.

articles.title_orig: In a First, Earth Has Stretch of 6 Days Over Warming Ceiling
articles.title_zh: In a First, Earth Has Stretch of 6 Days Over Warming Ceiling
articles.content_orig:
Earth just saw the most anomalously hot day ever on record
With the most powerful El Niño in living memory still gaining strength, this record could soon be surpassed
By Andrea Thompson edited by Claire Cameron
Amanda Montañez; Source: Copernicus Climate Change Service ( data )
Join Our Community of Science Lovers!
Earth just saw the most anomalously hot day ever measured on the planet. According to preliminary data from the Europe-based Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), Friday, November 20, 2026, was 2.12 degrees Celsius higher than the preindustrial average—or the time before humans began heating up Earth by burning fossil fuels.
The record stems from a combination of long-term, human-driven climate change and a blockbuster El Niño that is likely the strongest in the past 1,000 years. It comes as international negotiations at the COP31 climate summit have fallen apart, with no global agreement on how to rein in global warming.
Amanda Montañez; Source: Copernicus Climate Change Service ( data )
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
There are likely to be more days with an anomaly at or above 2 degrees C as this El Niño builds to its crescendo over roughly the next month. The next several months are also likely to be record hot. “I think we will likely see more days exceeding 2 degrees C over the next couple of months (possibly through March 2027),” says Zachary Labe, a scientist at Climate Central, a climate research nonprofit, “though I still expect this to be more a rarity than the norm when comparing every day.”
It’s possible 2026 will be the hottest year on record, besting 2024, though it will be close and could end in a tie. Because it takes time for the heat released by El Niño in the Pacific to affect global temperatures, 2027 will likely see the biggest heat effect and will almost certainly become the hottest year on record. Both 2026 and 2027 are expected to be more than 1.5 degrees C above preindustrial temperatures, a level so far only ever surpassed in 2024.
Under the landmark 2015 Paris climate agreement , which came out of the COP21 meeting, countries agreed to limit warming to “well below” 2 degrees C above preindustrial and to try to keep it under 1.5 degrees C. But the United Nations recently announced that the world will blow past the 1.5 degrees C mark , with global temperatures expected to hit 1.8 degrees C above preindustrial.
Surpassing the 2 degrees C benchmark for a day—or even a year—doesn’t mean the Paris Agreement limit has been permanently breached, because that considers the average temperature over many years. By that measure, the world has warmed by nearly 1.4 degrees C above preindustrial, according to the U.N.
The COP31 summit—to which the U.S. did not send an official delegation—ended without an agreement for a final deal. These documents nominally provide a blueprint for countries to follow in their efforts to lower greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to the changing climate.
In a statement, outgoing secretary-general António Guterres, who has been a vocal supporter of phasing out fossil fuels, noted his “profound frustration” at the summit’s outcome. “Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly,” Guterres said. “The world is now poised to exceed the globally-agreed limit of a 1.5 degree temperature rise. The window to keep that overshoot as short and shallow as possible is rapidly closing.”

articles.title_orig: Redesigned OLED MacBook Air Could Launch in 2027 or 2028
articles.title_zh: Redesigned OLED MacBook Air Could Launch in 2027 or 2028
articles.content_orig:
A MacBook Air with a new look could launch in late 2027 or 2028, Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman said in the latest episode of his Power On podcast. Apple plans to refresh the ‌MacBook Air‌ with M6 chips in early 2027 alongside the MacBook Neo 2, but that update won't include a new design.
A more extensive overhaul could follow later in 2027 or in 2028, and the ‌MacBook Air‌ could get an OLED display at that time.
MacBook Air is Apple's most popular computer, and they need to keep it very fresh. And so my anticipation is 2027, 2028 is when we're going to get the big MacBook Air overhaul. And I think OLED will be part of that conversation.
Apple last overhauled the ‌MacBook Air‌'s design in 2022, eliminating the prior wedge shape for a more uniform MacBook Pro-style chassis. The machine adopted a brighter Liquid Retina display with a notch for the camera, and a MagSafe charging port. In 2023, Apple added a 15-inch model, but since then, we've only gotten minor updates.
Apple just added ‌OLED‌ to the MacBook Pro with the launch of the 2026 PROLED models, so it's not clear whether the high-end display will trickle down to the ‌MacBook Air‌ that quickly. In prior reports , Gurman has leaned more toward the 2028 timeline than late 2027.
Pricing on the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ starts at $2,899, while the ‌MacBook Air‌ is one of Apple's more affordable notebooks and starts at $1,299. Apple would likely need to offer a high-end ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Air‌ alongside ‌MacBook Air‌ models with an LCD display to keep the price gap intact.

articles.title_orig: 2 California companies are buying Nvidia's most advanced chips. Those companies are actually Chinese-owned, a CBS News investigation reveals.
articles.title_zh: 2 California companies are buying Nvidia's most advanced chips. Those companies are actually Chinese-owned, a CBS News investigation reveals.
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia is selling its most cutting-edge chips to at least two companies that are U.S.-based, but are actually controlled by Chinese-owned firms, raising fresh questions about efforts to keep sensitive technology away from the nation's rivals, a CBS News investigation found.
One of the chip giant's "preferred partners" is a California company owned by a Chinese firm whose chief executive is a graduate of a Chinese military university, records show. Another California company was renamed after its Chinese-owned parent company was blacklisted.
Some of these U.S.-based, Chinese-owned firms have then leased or sold the advanced chips, used for artificial intelligence, to other companies in Southeast Asia, records show.
The world of computer chip exports is murky — and labyrinthine chains of custody have made it even more difficult to determine just how many of the most sensitive Nvidia chips are being exploited by China, experts told CBS News.
"It is a wake-up call for accountability, for properly resourcing the enforcement bodies, and for every leading private-sector tech company to map where it is exposed," said Mishel Kondi, a senior analyst at C4ADS, which specializes in using public data, from corporate filings to satellite imagery, to uncover sanctions violations and smuggling.
C4ADS, a Washington-based global security nonprofit also known as the Center for Advanced Defense Studies, examined corporate filings and other company ownership data at the request of CBS News. This story is based on dozens of corporate filings, court records and an investigation of Nvidia's corporate relationships dating back to 2023 — long before its CEO Jensen Huang and his behemoth chip company dominated the news cycle.
That explosive saga began 27 days ago when the news broke that Huang had been having an affair with Alice Huang — a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset. The Justice Department has said it has not reached a conclusion, and Beijing denies she is a spy. The company she ran, Megaspeed, a cloud computing company based in Singapore, is under investigation by the Justice Department for allegedly circumventing export bans by obtaining computer chips for use by China.
But Megaspeed , national security and trade experts say, is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the transfer of Nvidia chips to China. And elected officials are now asking questions like: How are Nvidia's chips getting to China? And what did Jensen Huang and his colleagues know about it?
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a senior Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement this week.
Nvidia had almost $20 billion in sales to China last year. The company can sell graphics cards for personal computers and server chips with lower processing power to China without a special license.
What is not allowed — and is under strict export controls — are the sales of Nvidia's most technologically advanced chips, which are powering the AI revolution.
But recent reporting, including from CBS News, has shown some of the highest end chips, called Blackwells, have made it into Chinese hands.
The circuitous trail traveled by Nvidia chips quickly gets muddy.
Take RiCloud AI, a data center company based in San Jose, California. RiCloud AI appears on Nvidia's list of "preferred partners" in the U.S., affording it preferential access to sales of high-end computer chips used for advanced AI models.
These are classified as American sales, according to Nvidia's public filings — with the chips going to RiCloud AI, Inc., a U.S. company.
But RiCloud AI's parent company is Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings Limited. That company is headquartered in Shenzhen, China, and is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange.
Yuxing's CEO and co-owner, Cong Yu, has a degree in National Defense Mobilization from the People's Liberation Army Command College, a university run by the Chinese military. Yu is also CEO of a related RiCloud company in California.
And Yuxing's chairman, Li Qiang, was previously chairman of data firm Global Switch Holdings, which was dropped as a data center provider by Australia's Department of Defense in June 2024 over national security concerns.
The U.S. government has not accused RiCloud and Yuxing of any wrongdoing.
By December 2025, just 10 weeks after it was incorporated, RiCloud AI had secured its partner status with Nvidia and has since become a "preferred" cloud partner, giving the company priority access to advanced chips, Nvidia's software and technical support. Nvidia has not responded to questions about what background checks it conducted before awarding the privileged status to RiCloud AI.
An examination of RiCloud AI's clients suggests that some seem like unorthodox customers for such high-powered technology. This year, for example, it signed a $120 million deal to lease 300 Nvidia B300 servers to a company in Taiwan that was primarily known for selling whisky.
Agencia Comercial Spirits was a small whisky importer with $609,000 in net income in 2025 when it listed on the Nasdaq as an AI company. This year it has made commitments for AI data center-related deals totaling between $488 and $598 million, after Li was appointed as chairman.
Agencia did not respond to a request for comment. In a February press release announcing its pivot into data centers, Agencia said the move was "part of a broader review of strategic opportunities outside its core whisky business."
Then there is California company Aivres, which is currently listed on Nvidia's website as an "elite" compute partner — the highest tier of relationship with the chip giant.
Aivres used to be called Inspur, the same name as its Chinese parent company. But when Inspur group firms in China were added to a federal blacklist of companies considered a security risk to the U.S. in March 2023, the California subsidiary changed its name and today still maintains its close relationship with Nvidia. Aivres itself is not on the blacklist.
Aivres, which produces data center servers housing Nvidia chips, exported at least $5.6 billion of advanced technology to Southeast Asia between April 2024 and February 2026, according to a New York Times analysis of trade records published two months ago.
Some $3 billion of those exports were for computers containing Nvidia's cutting-edge Blackwell chips, which are restricted from being exported to China, the Times reported.
The Aivres chips then went to two companies in Malaysia — Megaspeed and Aolani — providing cloud AI services to Chinese firms Alibaba and ByteDance, according to the Times.
Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm where Jensen Huang paramour Alice Huang was a top executive, was blacklisted by the U.S. government this week, in the wake of the scandal. The company denies any wrongdoing.
The Pentagon put Alibaba on a blacklist in June, claiming it used advanced chips to help the Chinese military. The company denies it and sued the government over the blacklisting, winning a preliminary injunction last month.
The servers owned by Inspur — Aivres' parent company — are used in China by the country's military, according to the U.S. government . Aivres did not respond to requests for comment.
Another of Nvidia's elite U.S. partners has surfaced in a recent $300 million chip smuggling case, though it has not been accused of wrongdoing.
Earlier this year, a California businessman named Greg Lui was indicted for allegedly smuggling export-controlled chips to China via Malaysia and Singapore in 2023 and 2024. He has pleaded not guilty.
Records reviewed by CBS News link Lui to 2CRSi, an Nvidia elite partner in the U.S. that is a branch of a French-owned company making AI data servers.

President Donald Trump took credit Monday for the stock market rebound following his intervention to get disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reinstated , hailing it a “great day” for the country.
Two days later — the same day that the Trump administration unveiled a wave of new tariffs on China and Europe — the president is blaming the Democrats for the stock market dip.
“Stocks are down sharply because of the November Third Election results,” Trump posted Wednesday on Truth Social. “I wasn’t on the Ballot, but if I was, the results, just like all three times before, would have been much different, and the Stock Market, and your 401-k’s, would be BOOMING.”
“I told you so!!!” he gloated, in contrast to his celebratory tone earlier in the week after he personally waded into the leadership crisis at Nvidia and helped restore Huang as CEO of the billionaire AI-chip-making company.
Nvidia’s stock suffered after Huang stepped down as CEO on November 12 following a confession that he had been unfaithful to his wife of more than 40 years.
“I watched that and, you know, I better get involved,” Trump reacted Monday on CNBC. “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”
After Huang was reinstated, Nvidia’s stock soared 31 percent as Wall Street enjoyed its best day since April 2025.
“I believe my intervention was very important,” the president said. He explained that he held off from interfering previously but decided to speak to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” over the weekend.
“And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was to me a very important part of our country,” he said. “When the stock starts dropping 40, 50 percent, it was a lot easier for me to do it yesterday.”
Trump acknowledged the situation could change.
“I’ve seen some pretty good comebacks, but I tell you, what you have to have for a comeback really is longevity,” he told CNBC. “So, you know, we can’t call it a comeback one day, but I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company.”
At the end of the call with the outlet, Trump celebrated “a great day for the market” and “for the country” but his tune changed Wednesday – a pattern that did not go unnoticed by his critics on social media.
“Stocks go up: Trump did it,” the progressive MediasTouch outlet posted on X. “Stocks go down: Democrats did it.”
“Didn't he take credit for the stocks going up on Monday?” another left-leaning account quipped.
“Maybe stocks are down because the U.S. economy has staked the future of itself and all of humanity on a bunch of greedy maladapted tech bros who can’t keep it in their pants,” another X user posted.
On November 4, the day after Trump and the Republicans suffered sweeping losses in the midterm elections, he posted that the stock market had “hit another Record High” on Truth Social. “Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!” he bragged.
But the next day, he said the stock market “suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election.”
“It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this. Your 401(k)s have, therefore, dropped. Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats,” he posted .

articles.content_orig:
Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly's asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil's assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC.
The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said.
The deal transfers Lukoil's international refineries and other production assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the U.S.-led group, the sources said. It also includes retail gas stations in the U.S., Europe and Asia, they said.
The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control is expected to sign off on the deal but final approval is still needed, the sources said. The deal would give the U.S.-led group about 350,000 barrels per day of production.
The agreement would allow Europe to buy fuel such as diesel previously produced by Lukoil through the U.S.-led group rather than Russia.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Sabrina Valle and Tom Wilson
NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Global markets retreated on Wednesday with riskier assets under pressure after the Trump administration proposed sweeping new tariffs on 14 trading partners.
US stocks, hammered in the morning, partially recovered in the afternoon ‌from early losses as investors bought the dip ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The Dow closed higher and the Nasdaq and S&P ‌500 ended slightly lower.
US technology shares led declines amid concerns about inflation and a hawkish Federal Reserve, while investors assessed the implications of the tariffs for global supply chains and economic ​growth. Treasury prices rose as investors sought safe-haven assets.
MSCI's global stocks index fell 0.60% and Nvidia shed more than 8% during the day before closing down 3.91%.
Oliver Pursche, senior vice president at Wealthspire Advisors, said bargain hunters were stepping in ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, adding that "investors are taking advantage of some of those discrepancies."
The Nasdaq was down more than 4% earlier in the session before closing down 0.62%, with the S&P 500 falling 0.25% and the Dow up 0.33%.
The ‌selloff was mirrored elsewhere, with Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan ⁠down 1.99% and emerging market stocks falling 2.8%.
"We still have not dealt with the fresh shock of Nvidia and tech and now we have tariffs," said Aneeka Gupta, an equity strategist at WisdomTree.
"Markets are contending with AI, central banks ⁠remain hawkish, and then if we get a renewal of tariffs that adds volatility in markets."
European shares, which had traded higher earlier on gains in personal and household goods and retail stocks, later reversed course. The pan-European STOXX 600 fell 1.06%.
Earlier in the day, the broad selloff, combined with lower bond yields, signaled growing concern that ​escalating ​trade barriers could weigh on global growth and corporate earnings. By the close of ​the US stock market, copper and aluminum prices had risen, ‌and bitcoin had gained 0.81%.
US Treasury yields declined on Wednesday but were off their earlier lows. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 6.2 basis points to 4.84% and was on pace for its seventh daily drop in the past eight sessions.
Nvidia gave up part of its gains from earlier this week, leaving the stock down about 10% since Monday, when CEO Jensen Huang's return sparked a 31.5% rally. S&P Global Ratings put the company at risk of a rating downgrade.
Data showed US consumer confidence increased by more than expected in November to its highest level in nearly ‌two years. Separately, data showed the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the ​third quarter, and inflation increased further in October.
The dollar index, which measures the US ​currency against a basket of major peers including the yen and ​euro, fell 0.14%, while the euro was up 0.11% to $1.09.
The inflation and growth data reinforced expectations that the Federal ‌Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in ​early 2027.
Euro zone government bond yields fell ​as the slide in US equities drove investors towards the relative safety of sovereign debt. Germany's benchmark 10-year Bund yield fell 4.73 basis points to 3.218%, from 3.266% late on Tuesday.
Brent crude futures LCOc1 settled $3.21, or 3.5%, higher at $94.61 a barrel, after Yemen's Houthis said they ​had attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery. [O/R]
Trading volume was ‌low, and US markets will be closed Thursday.
(Reporting by Sabrina Valle and Caroline Valetkevitch in New York and Tom Wilson in ​London; additional reporting by Chuck Mikolajczak in New York, Dhara Ranasinghe in London, Gregor Stuart Hunter in Singapore and Roger Tung ​in Taipei. Editing by DJ Yap, Gareth Jones, Mark Potter and Deepa Babington)

articles.title_orig: S&P warns Nvidia's board may be compromised, puts chipmaker's rating on downgrade watch
articles.title_zh: S&P warns Nvidia's board may be compromised, puts chipmaker's rating on downgrade watch
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch over the next 90 days if the company continues to have "deficiencies" in its management and governance framework, S&P Global Ratings said in the wake of the Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.
"News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," S&P said in a Wednesday note .
Nvidia currently holds an AA rating, the third-highest level.
S&P has placed the chipmaker on "CreditWatch with negative implications," though any potential downgrade would be limited to one notch, to AA-, unless investigations or disclosures lead the agency to conclude that Nvidia's reputation or future prospects have also been harmed.
A downgrade can pressure bond prices, push yields higher and raise borrowing costs. Nvidia priced $25 billion of investment-grade senior notes in June, with maturities from 2028 through 2056, shortly after S&P upgraded the company from AA- to AA.
Nvidia has about $32.5 billion of bonds in the U.S. high-grade corporate bond index, according to Bloomberg.
S&P's Wednesday note follows Moody's Ratings changing its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive on Nov. 18, citing governance concerns, and leaving that outlook unchanged after Huang's return on Monday.
In its note, S&P cited the "long tenure" of certain board members as a reason their independence may be "compromised" and said Nvidia's management and governance risk was "rising."
The ratings agency added that it remained unaware of any remedial action taken by the board to address what could be "meaningful" management and governance deficiencies.
Chairman Harvey Jones and early investor Tench Coxe have served on Nvidia's board since 1993, while Brooke Seawell joined in 1997. Mark Stevens served from 1993 to 2006 and rejoined the board in 2008.
S&P also flagged questions around geopolitical risk management and internal controls arising from Nvidia's exposure to China.
"While Nvidia management has delivered significant returns for its stakeholders over decades, weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the "key man" risk to the forefront," S&P's Andrew Chang and David Tsui said.
Chang and Tsui noted that Huang's resignation and subsequent reinstatement did not resolve questions about the board's oversight of executive conduct.
The agency also intends to meet with Nvidia's board and management to discuss plans to address those deficiencies, particularly around "board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession plan."
Huang returned less than two weeks after Jones said Nvidia's directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back, sending Nvidia shares up as much as 36% during Monday's session.
Nvidia shares are down about 12.5% since Monday's close.

articles.title_orig: Vance says Jensen Huang won't need a pardon as scrutiny of Nvidia scandal builds in Washington
articles.title_zh: Vance says Jensen Huang won't need a pardon as scrutiny of Nvidia scandal builds in Washington
articles.content_orig:
Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche told him Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation.
"I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters in Ohio on Wednesday after being asked what assurances he had gotten that Huang was not under investigation. "Not even that he was about to be prosecuted; that he's under no investigation."
Vance spoke two days after President Donald Trump told CNBC in an interview that an investigation had been done.
Trump was asked what Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws.
"They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said Monday.
Reuters reported Wednesday that the Department of Justice did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his reinstatement as CEO.
Blanche had concluded there was no evidence Huang had broken any laws based on investigations into Nvidia clients Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed, according to the report.
The DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Reuters report. And the White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Vance saying Huang was under no investigation when Trump had said there was one. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about Vance's remarks.
Blanche on Tuesday dodged questions about whether there had been an investigation.
"What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him," Blanche said after being asked whether the DOJ had investigated Huang and, if so, what were the results of the probe.
Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, after the chipmaker's board of directors said it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government" that Huang was not a national security risk. Trump took credit for Huang's reinstatement in the interview with CNBC shortly after Nvidia's announcement.
Huang resigned following The New York Times reporting multiple affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing and who was an executive for the Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed.
The reporting added fuel to allegations that Nvidia should have known its artificial intelligence chips were being diverted to China and being used by Chinese companies, violating U.S. export laws.
"The product they create is a very important part of us staying ahead of the SI arms race with China. We really do care about ensuring those chips do not fall into the wrong hands," Vance said, using the Trump administration's preferred acronym for AI, which the president calls "super intelligence."
"We actually see this is an opportunity for Nvidia to focus on complying with American export controls, and we think Jensen Huang is going to take that very seriously," Vance continued.
"We received the assurances that he was not under any significant — he was under no investigation — and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence," Vance said.
On Tuesday, Trump left the door open to pardon Huang in an interview with the New York Post , but Vance said on Wednesday that the CEO doesn't need one.
"I don't think he needs a pardon at all," Vance said. "I haven't seen any evidence again that he committed a crime. And if there is evidence that he committed a crime, then that's up to relevant authorities to actually bring a prosecution against him."
Huang is scheduled to appear for a closed-door interview with House committees about his dealings with Megaspeed on Tuesday. At the same time, Nvidia will hold its annual conference where it showcases new technology in Washington.
— Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Norse Atlantic ceases flights amid cash crunch
articles.title_zh: Norse Atlantic ceases flights amid cash crunch
articles.content_orig:
Some Norse Atlantic flights were cancelled on Wednesday and Thursday, raising concerns about the future of the low-cost long-haul airline shortly after it warned that it was in a "critical financial situation."
Shares of Norse closed 53.3% lower on Wednesday after plunging as much as 86% during the session.
The airline had been set to operate two Pakistan International Airlines flights Wednesday under a wet-lease agreement, in which one airline provides the aircraft and crew to another. The agreement had only been signed in early October.
But PK786 from London to Islamabad and PK710 from Manchester to Lahore were cancelled because of "an unexpected operational suspension," the Pakistani flag carrier said on X.
Norse Atlantic has yet to make an official statement on its operational status. Checks by CNBC showed the airline was still selling tickets as at 1:30 a.m. Oslo time on Thursday.
PIA said it would operate the routes using its own Boeing 777 aircraft from Wednesday.
Norse's own flight Z0 783 from London Gatwick to Orlando was also shown as canceled Wednesday on live air traffic website Flightradar24. London Gatwick's website listed the flight's status for Thursday as "enquire airline."
In a bid to stave off financial troubles, Norse cut 75 jobs in May as part of an effort to reduce costs by $50 million, after Eivind Roald replaced founder Bjorn Tore Larsen as CEO in November last year.
The Norwegian carrier said Wednesday that its situation depended on securing financing for short-term liquidity needs and that it was in discussions about a potential strategic takeover.
"Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," the airline said.
India's largest airline, low-cost carrier IndiGo, entered an agreement with Norse Atlantic in early 2025 to lease six 787-9 aircraft as it launched flights to Europe and Britain ahead of the arrival of its own widebody planes.
The agreement concluded at the end of October this year, with IndiGo citing airspace constraints, elevated fuel costs and currency pressures.
At its peak in 2024, Norse Atlantic had 4,822 scheduled flights. That number dipped to 4,695 in 2025 and 2,565 in 2026, according to aviation analyst Cirium. The airline had 122 flights scheduled for November this year.
Norse Atlantic CEO Roald told CNBC in May that he was not "overly concerned" about access to fuel and said the airline had no indication at the time that the crisis would have an immediate impact. The airline said in October that it was continuing to operate at reduced capacity because of "prolonged high fuel prices."

articles.title_orig: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
articles.title_zh: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
articles.content_orig:
At least 31 people were ⁠⁠killed, and ⁠⁠another 21 were injured when a vehicle carrying ‌‌petroleum products overturned and caught fire on a major ring ⁠⁠⁠⁠road in the Egyptian capital, Cairo, the ⁠Ministry of Health said on Wednesday.
The fire broke out above a tunnel in the al-Warak neighbourhood of Giza’s Imbabah district. The ring road connects key highways across Greater Cairo, linking the governorates of Cairo, ‌‌Giza and Qalyubia.
Local media reported that a truck swerved and hit the central reservation as it overturned, triggering an explosion. The fire has since been extinguished, according to local media.
Egypt’s public prosecutor announced an investigation into the crash and ordered the collection of DNA samples from the victims’ bodies. The judicial office also said 27 vehicles were burned.
The Health Ministry said 39 ambulances were sent to the site of the incident and that the injured were transferred to nearby hospitals.
Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said he would head to the crash scene himself.
The official spokesman for the Egyptian presidency said President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi “expresses his sincere condolences and sincere sympathy to the families of the victims” and wished them a speedy recovery.
According to an Egyptian Cabinet statement, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly offered his condolences to the victims’ families and ordered that their medical expenses be covered by the state.

articles.title_orig: How the Trump administration determined Jensen Huang is not a national security threat
articles.title_zh: How the Trump administration determined Jensen Huang is not a national security threat
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
WASHINGTON — In May 2017, just months into his first term, President Trump welcomed Russians into the Oval Office . At that meeting, he disclosed highly classified intelligence collected by Israeli partners that risked compromising a coveted allied source.
In the years to come, he went on to resist security protocols around his personal communications, plowing through the clearance process for his close aides and family. He shared classified reconnaissance imagery on Twitter. He removed some of the most sensitive secrets in the U.S. government after leaving office, storing them in a bathroom at Mar-a-Lago , and at an event there openly discussed the whereabouts of U.S. nuclear submarines.
Now, the president is once again under fire for dismissing counterintelligence concerns, this time over a Chinese espionage campaign targeting Nvidia , the world’s largest AI chipmaker and one of the nation’s most valuable companies.
This week, Trump succeeded in persuading Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang as its leader, despite  Huang’s admission to engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The president cited the stock market’s reaction to Huang’s firing as one of his leading motivations.
Criticism came from across the Republican spectrum, from the party’s old guard to some of Trump’s most loyal supporters.
“I would have hoped the president had other tools for stimulating the AI-driven stock market than rewarding Chinese high-tech espionage,” said John D. Woodward Jr., a former CIA officer and senior Defense Department official now at Boston University.
Intelligence officials sounded an alarm last year over the Huang affair, raising concern at the CIA and prompting Marco Rubio, the national security advisor and secretary of state, to issue a warning to Trump. The president requested more information, but chose not to act after a preliminary review failed to identify a smoking gun that Huang had passed valuable information to the mistress, officials said.
Still, intelligence officials told lawmakers this week that Huang’s love interest, named Alice Huang, did in fact pass information to Chinese officials while the affair was ongoing.
Alice Huang had been a top executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based firm accused of purchasing advanced Nvidia chips to then siphon to China, bypassing U.S. export restrictions.
Advanced computer chips are the core of a competition between the United States and China as the dueling superpowers sprint for supremacy in artificial intelligence.
Trump has repeatedly said there is no acceptable alternative to an American victory in that race. But concern has grown across party lines that Trump has become reticent to confront China over its espionage attempts targeting U.S. companies at the technological frontier.
“Let me get this straight,” Mitt Romney, a former Republican senator from Utah and the 2012 GOP presidential nominee, wrote on social media this week. “We rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they’d need to get ahead of us.”
“Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse,” he added.
But Trump has been dismissive of intelligence concerns surrounding national security before.
Throughout his first term, Trump repeatedly rejected the unanimous assessment of U.S. intelligence agencies that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election to help him win. Most notoriously, at a 2018 news conference in Helsinki alongside Vladimir Putin, Trump said he trusted the Russian president’s word over the conclusions of his own intelligence community.
“My people came to me, Dan Coats came to me and some others, they said they think it’s Russia,” Trump said at the time, referring to his director of national intelligence. “I have President Putin — he just said it’s not Russia. I will say this: I don’t see any reason why it would be.”
“So I have great confidence in my intelligence people,” he added, “but I will tell you that President Putin was extremely strong and powerful in his denial today.”
Last spring, on his first of two visits to China this year, Trump told reporters that espionage from Beijing did not concern him.
“They’re talking about the spying. Well, we do it too,” Trump said aboard Air Force One, shortly after White House staff threw burner phones off the plane before takeoff. “We spy like hell on them, too.”
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said that the Nvidia co-founder and chief executive has been “exonerated” in a preliminary “study” of the episode. Huang did not pose a threat to national security by leading the company, Trump told the board.
On Tuesday, the U.S. attorney general, Todd Blanche, refused to say whether Huang would be investigated over the affair, questioning to reporters whether such a probe would be necessary.
“They did ask for assurance on the national security threat, and we gave them assurance, at least with everything we know,” Trump said, “and we know a lot.”
“He’s apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate,” he added. “That was probably — that’s what brought it to such a level. Because sex sells, fellas!”

articles.title_orig: Trump's new tariffs would put rates right back where they were before the Supreme Court stepped in
articles.title_zh: Trump's new tariffs would put rates right back where they were before the Supreme Court stepped in
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration has announced new tariffs on 14 major trading partners , including China and the European Union, claiming that excess production has given them an unfair advantage.
The proposed levies come after a months-long investigation into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan, launched after the Supreme Court struck down United States President Donald Trump’s sweeping global tariffs in February.
The highest tariff rate announced on Wednesday would hit China the hardest, at 20 percent, adding to the roughly 25 percent duties that Trump imposed on China during his first term.
The proposed tariffs would not apply to about $30bn of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.
Washington has long accused China of subsidising its industries and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products, allegations that Beijing has once again denied.
“The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, urging the world’s two top economies to maintain stable relations.
Other US trading partners facing proposed new tariffs include India, Japan, South Korea, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
Mexico and Norway were also part of the probe but were excluded from the new round of tariffs because investigations into their trade practices are still ongoing.
The tariff announcement follows an eight-month investigation initiated by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.
“The administration’s use of Section 301 is cynical,” Gregory Shaffer, professor of international law at the Georgetown University Law Center, told Al Jazeera. “It launched these investigations in order to support the president’s aim to set tariffs globally and to modify them at any time at the president’s will, and thus strip Congress of the authority to set tariff rates under the taxing power set forth in the Constitution.”
In a separate announcement, the White House also announced a proposed 10 percent tariff on finished aircraft made by Brazilian planemaker Embraer, whose jets are widely used by US regional carriers operating under brands including United Express, Delta Connection and American Eagle. Finished aircraft are Brazil’s fourth-biggest export to the US.
The US also plans to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices, according to a senior US official.
Several governments have reacted to the new tariff announcement, as has the European Union.
“The EU takes note of the publication by the US of preliminary findings pursuant to its Section 301 investigation concerning structural excess capacity in manufacturing sectors,” European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill told Al Jazeera.
“We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Gill added.
The Swiss government has also reacted, saying that it rejects the allegations stemming from the investigations.
“The timing right before the G20 [in mid-December] sets up those meetings as an opportunity for negotiation and increases risk of both inflationary pressures and macro volatility in 2027, reducing some of the benefit from easing gas prices,” Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.
Norway has praised the decision.
“We have been clear throughout the process that Norway does not have policies that contribute to overcapacity. Norwegian companies produce in response to market demand,” Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said.
US markets fell on news of the new tariffs.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.6 percent after tumbling more than 4 percent in early trading, while the S&P 500 closed down 0.25 percent.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.3 percent, reversing earlier losses.
The price of gold – which is considered a safe investment in times of economic uncertainty – fell by more than 3 percent to its lowest level in more than a year. However, in addition to tariffs, the price was influenced by inflation data released on Wednesday which showed a 0.3 percent rise in one of the US Federal Reserve’s key metrics for assessing the rate of inflation. Higher inflation increases the chances of a rise in interest rates, which in turn weighs on the metal.
Bond yields in both the US and Europe dropped on Wednesday.
Germany’s 10-year bond yield, which is the benchmark for the eurozone, slid by 4.5 basis points to 3.2 percent, while the US 10-year Treasury note yield stumbled by 6.8 basis points to 4.834 percent, putting it on pace for its seventh daily drop over the past eight sessions.
